extraction.body: Discover-Tech’s Controlium software lets clients mass-profile internet users then covertly hack targets, say researchers at University of Toronto Discover-Tech’s Controlium software lets clients mass-profile internet users then covertly hack targets, say researchers at University of Toronto An Israeli advertising agency has been serving millions of online adverts that allow “zero-click” spyware to be used against targets, researchers at a Canadian university have said . Citizen Lab, a digital investigations research unit at the University of Toronto, said it believed dozens of devices at the Qatari broadcaster Al Jazeera had been compromised by spyware delivered through ads run by Discover-Tech, which describes itself as a specialised digital advertising agency. According to Citizen Lab, Discover-Tech operates a software platform called Controlium that allows its clients to “mass-profile and deanonymise” internet users then covertly hack targets with third-party spyware. Unlike infections that rely on people interacting with links or files, the spyware requires no interaction from the victim to be installed, making it a new delivery technique, Citizen Lab says. The infections happen without a user’s knowledge, and in a matter of seconds, according to Citizen Lab. “[The online advertising] ecosystem is being weaponised at a massive scale to profile millions of users, then silently infect targets with zero-click mercenary spyware,” the report says. According to the report, Controlium is able to harvest a user’s identity and IP address when the user is shown a seemingly benign custom-created ad – for example, for a digital game or a telecoms service. If the user has been selected as a target for hacking, a mercenary spyware firm can then send a malicious code containing spyware to their device, the researchers say. They say that millions of users worldwide have been served ads by Discover-Tech since 2024, including in Yemen, Brazil, Mexico and Czechia. “It’s disastrous that major ad vendors and organisations apparently were neither able to detect nor prevent the company’s malicious advertising operations for years,” said Wolfie Christl, a researcher at Citizen Lab. “The way the online advertising ecosystem works today is a security threat for states, the private sector, civil society and everyone else alike.” According to Citizen Lab, Controlium acts as a “facilitator” for third-party spyware firms that have targeted “government officials, journalists, businesspeople, activists, academics and embassy workers”. Citizen Lab claims it can deliver spyware that can access everything on the device of a target, extracting messages, photos and emails, recording calls and secretly activating microphones. The full extent of the targeting allegedly enabled by Discover-Tech is unknown. Citizen Lab’s findings join mounting evidence that the opaque arrangements underpinning the world of online advertising can be leveraged for surveillance. “There has been a lot of buzz that online ads can be used to identify and automatically hack targets with pinpoint precision, but now for the first time, we have concrete technical evidence showing this process in action,” said Bill Marczak, a researcher at Citizen Lab. Discover-Tech has been approached for comment. These bids are based on the user’s profile, which can include information about their device and data compiled on them by tracking their activity across the web. For example, companies given the profile of a 35-year-old interested in sports betting and crypto might bid to show that individual an advertisement for an energy drink. There is little regulation on this automated online market, and there is growing evidence that it is being exploited by malevolent actors. Reuters has reported that billions of dollars’ worth of Meta’s ad revenue comes from ads for scams, illegal gambling, pornography and other banned content. In the US, ICE and other government agencies have bought software that uses ad tech data to track people’s movements. “Cybersecurity agencies, regulators and lawmakers in the US, Europe and other regions must urgently step in. They must investigate the involved companies and fix the systemic risks that enable malicious ad targeting,” said Christl.

sources.title: ‘Nightmare Scenario’: Zero-Click Spyware Is Infecting Phones via Targeted Ads
passages: “The risk of having your device infected with spyware simply by using a website or app that displays ads is a nightmare scenario,” says Wolfie Christl, a senior Citizen Lab researcher.
During 2024 and 2025, Citizen Lab concluded that 45 devices belonging to the news outlet Al Jazeera were targeted with zero-click attacks delivered by ads.
Zero-click hacks are a holy grail for attackers and catastrophic for victims, because they can automatically install malware on devices without requiring any interaction or missteps from the target.

In fact, they might not even see any ad at all.” The situation is so concerning, he notes, because there isn’t much that people can do to protect themselves from zero-click ad attacks other than blocking ads as thoroughly as possible on all websites and platforms—a fact that intelligence agencies like the NSA and CIA seem to know all too well.
The researchers say that the targeted ads were issued by the Israeli-founded marketing firm Discover-Tech and distributed spyware attributed to the Israeli developer Candiru.
Citizen Lab believes this to be the first detailed technical evidence made publicly available of sophisticated spyware infecting devices via digital ads.

The process has been a privacy nightmare for years, with murky data brokers selling people’s personal information, and law enforcement agencies and hostile nations buying it to track or target people.

Google, which operates one of the world’s largest advertising businesses, terminated Discover-Tech’s registration after collaborating with Citizen Lab and researchers from the cybersecurity firm Confiant and confirming a spyware link.

extraction.body: Dubbing the attacks “AdFection,” the researchers documented a campaign in which an Israeli-registered advertising firm allegedly connected to the servers linked to a spyware company and infected dozens of devices with its invasive malware. Citizen Lab believes this to be the first detailed technical evidence made publicly available of sophisticated spyware infecting devices via digital ads. Zero-click hacks are a holy grail for attackers and catastrophic for victims, because they can automatically install malware on devices without requiring any interaction or missteps from the target. When sophisticated hackers have deployed rare zero-click attacks in recent years, they have often exploited vulnerabilities in mobile messaging and communication apps to infect victims. But attackers have also exploited the sprawling infrastructure of the online ad ecosystem to distribute malware, sometimes with little or no interaction needed from victims. Evidence of the zero-click spyware campaign that Citizen Lab’s researchers uncovered shows the two threats merging, underscoring the extent and urgency of the risk. “AdFection allows operators to automatically hack specific individuals with mercenary spyware as they use apps or browse the internet,” says Bill Marczak, a senior researcher at Citizen Lab. In fact, they might not even see any ad at all.” The situation is so concerning, he notes, because there isn’t much that people can do to protect themselves from zero-click ad attacks other than blocking ads as thoroughly as possible on all websites and platforms—a fact that intelligence agencies like the NSA and CIA seem to know all too well. “The risk of having your device infected with spyware simply by using a website or app that displays ads is a nightmare scenario,” says Wolfie Christl, a senior Citizen Lab researcher. During 2024 and 2025, Citizen Lab concluded that 45 devices belonging to the news outlet Al Jazeera were targeted with zero-click attacks delivered by ads. The researchers say that the targeted ads were issued by the Israeli-founded marketing firm Discover-Tech and distributed spyware attributed to the Israeli developer Candiru. Infected devices had contact with domains linked to Discover-Tech and then connected to infrastructure associated with Candiru, according to Citizen Lab’s analysis. (Al Jazeera, which participated in the investigation and shared device logs with Citizen Lab researchers, did not respond to a request for comment.) “The ability to push individualized, arbitrary content at specific users is a hallmark of the modern online ads ecosystem, and is perfectly suited to the mercenary spyware industry,” Marczak says. “Until this architecture changes, or ad companies get serious about customer vetting, we’re going to keep seeing this kind of abuse.” Emails and messages sent to Discover-Tech and its CEO by WIRED did not receive a response before publication. Google, which operates one of the world’s largest advertising businesses, terminated Discover-Tech’s registration after collaborating with Citizen Lab and researchers from the cybersecurity firm Confiant and confirming a spyware link. “Following a joint investigation with Citizen Lab and Confiant, Google blocked Discover-Tech from our ad platforms for systematically violating our policies,” a Google spokesperson says. “We also set up Safe Browsing warnings to help protect people if they navigate to websites linked to this group.” The European branch of the Interactive Advertising Bureau (IAB), an ad industry body, confirmed to WIRED that it has suspended Discover-Tech from its global vendor list, known as the GVL. The company was suspended by IAB Europe following an audit of its policies, it says. “Further confirmation of the findings regarding spyware could also justify a definitive expulsion from the GVL,” a spokesperson for IAB Europe says. A spokesperson for Beeswax, an online advertising industry company owned by Comcast, says in a statement: “Beeswax removed Discovery-Tech from our platform following recent activity and independent validation by a third-party security specialist. We maintain a zero-tolerance policy for malicious advertising.” Often when you see ads online or in apps, they’re displayed following a complex process known as real-time bidding—essentially an automated auction where advertisers place bids to show you specific ads. The process has been a privacy nightmare for years, with murky data brokers selling people’s personal information, and law enforcement agencies and hostile nations buying it to track or target people. The Citizen Lab researchers say that Discover-Tech operates an advertising platform, Controlium, that can allow its users to “de-anonymize, fingerprint, and automatically infect devices” once an ad appears. Overall, the researchers estimate that millions of devices were directed to Candiru’s servers, where they could be profiled. By analyzing ad-bidding records that were publicly exposed on the Discover-Tech website, the Citizen Lab researchers say, ads linked to the firm with attacker script tags were shown in more than 70,000 mobile apps and more than 120,000 websites between March and June this year. Multiple apps, the researchers say, displayed more than a million ads linked to Discover-Tech. The firm’s ads weren’t necessarily all weaponized to potentially distribute spyware, but the researchers say that, in general, they have seen Discover-Tech ad impressions on government and national-security-linked networks around the world. Previous zero-click targeted ad campaigns that distribute spyware have rarely surfaced publicly, but the Citizen Lab researchers say this is likely a symptom of ad infrastructure being so extensively trusted and incorporated in all aspects of digital life without specific oversight. “The network logs from Al Jazeera were key in understanding the ad-based nature of that attack,” Marczak says. “If a user’s personal device were targeted, say, while they were connected to their home Wi-Fi or mobile data, there’s not going to be the same level of network monitoring there. So I think the lack of prior reporting is probably mainly a visibility issue: Defenders have to be in the right place at the right time, looking at the right data.” Speaking generally about threats that can result from the sheer ubiquity of the digital ad ecosystem, Jason Kint, CEO of the digital media trade organization Digital Content Next (WIRED parent company Condé Nast is a member), says these kinds of attacks are both plausible and damaging. “Although rare and sophisticated, I wouldn’t be entirely surprised to learn about zero-click attacks through ads,” Kint says. “Anything that goes directly against users’ expectations or lowers the trust in the open web is deeply concerning.”

sources.title: An Israeli firm is sending spyware through online ads, researchers say
passages: An Israeli ad tech firm worked with spyware companies to infect devices, including at Al Jazeera, by simply showing users an online ad, according to a joint investigation by security researchers at Citizen Lab and Confiant.

The ad firm, called Discover-Tech, presents itself as a typical online advertising agency, but researchers say it actually provides a pipeline for hacking groups to plant malicious ads across the web.
One of the groups Discover-Tech works with is Candiru, an Israeli spyware company that has been blacklisted by the US government.

extraction.body: An Israeli ad tech firm worked with spyware companies to infect devices, including at Al Jazeera, by simply showing users an online ad, according to a joint investigation by security researchers at Citizen Lab and Confiant. It’s the first time researchers have found technical evidence of a zero-click attack — a form of hacking that requires no action by users — delivered through targeted advertising, as reported earlier by NBC News. The ad firm, called Discover-Tech, presents itself as a typical online advertising agency, but researchers say it actually provides a pipeline for hacking groups to plant malicious ads across the web. It operates a platform known as “Controlium” that allows its spyware partners to “precisely profile and de-anonymize millions of individuals, fingerprint their devices, and target them with a form of zero-click hacking,” according to the investigation. It also allows them to “select a user for infection or profiling” using their IP address, mobile ad ID, or browser identifier. One of the groups Discover-Tech works with is Candiru, an Israeli spyware company that has been blacklisted by the US government. In 2024 and 2025, Discover-Tech ads delivered Candiru-linked spyware to Al Jazeera, a Qatar-based news network. Researchers say the companies targeted “at least” 45 devices at the news outlet in 2024 and 2025. Citizen Lab and Confiant call on the advertising industry to ramp up security on their platforms. Google and the Comcast-owned advertising company Beeswax have since removed Discover-Tech from their platforms, while IAB Europe suspended the company from its list of approved vendors, Reuters reports. Researchers also recommend that users at high risk of targeting use ad blockers, disable ad tracking, and regularly reset mobile ad IDs.

sources.title: Zero-click ads used to infect journalists’ devices with spyware, investigation finds - The Globe and Mail
passages: Geoffrey York is one of the longest-serving foreign correspondents in Canada, and one of The Globe and Mail's longest-serving journalists.

After a 13-year career in bureaus and beats in Canada, he has worked in foreign bureaus since 1994, beginning in Moscow (1994 to 2002), then in Beijing (2002 to 2008) and then in Johannesburg (2009 to the present).
Researchers say that in 2024 and 2025, at least 45 devices within Al Jazeera were targets of 'zero-click attacks' that they link with 'high confidence' to spyware from Candiru, an Israeli company.

The Citizen Lab, which researches how technology is used to threaten human rights and security, says in a 72-page report published Thursday that this is the “first public technical confirmation of a zero-click mercenary spyware attack delivered via targeted advertising.”
All comments are subject to the Community Guidelines and are moderated. \n

“It’s kind of a nightmare because it shows that devices can potentially be infected by spyware mercenaries, spyware companies, by just viewing an ad on a website or in a mobile app silently,” said Wolfie Christl, a co-author of the report who is based in Vienna.
The spyware was deployed through targeted online advertisements.
Previously, Janice spent nearly five years in The Globe’s Ottawa bureau, where her coverage focused on politics and immigration.

While the Al Jazeera journalists were directly targeted, the researchers uncovered that Discover-Tech ads were “shown on devices in national-security-sensitive networks around the world,” including those of defence ministries, militaries, national cybersecurity agencies, media organizations and intergovernmental and security organizations such as NATO.

coreStoryFacts.text: An Israeli advertising agency has been serving millions of online adverts that allow “zero-click” spyware to be used against targets, researchers at a Canadian university have said .
Citizen Lab claims it can deliver spyware that can access everything on the device of a target, extracting messages, photos and emails, recording calls and secretly activating microphones.

Citizen Lab, a digital investigations research unit at the University of Toronto, said it believed dozens of devices at the Qatari broadcaster Al Jazeera had been compromised by spyware delivered through ads run by Discover-Tech, which describes itself as a specialised digital advertising agency.
“The risk of having your device infected with spyware simply by using a website or app that displays ads is a nightmare scenario,” says Wolfie Christl, a senior Citizen Lab researcher.
During 2024 and 2025, Citizen Lab concluded that 45 devices belonging to the news outlet Al Jazeera were targeted with zero-click attacks delivered by ads.
Zero-click hacks are a holy grail for attackers and catastrophic for victims, because they can automatically install malware on devices without requiring any interaction or missteps from the target.

In fact, they might not even see any ad at all.” The situation is so concerning, he notes, because there isn’t much that people can do to protect themselves from zero-click ad attacks other than blocking ads as thoroughly as possible on all websites and platforms—a fact that intelligence agencies like the NSA and CIA seem to know all too well.

Citizen Lab, a digital investigations research unit at the University of Toronto, said it believed dozens of devices at the Qatari broadcaster Al Jazeera had been compromised by spyware delivered through ads run by Discover-Tech, which describes itself as a specialised digital advertising agency. According to Citizen Lab, Discover-Tech operates a software platform called Controlium that allows its clients to “mass-profile and deanonymise” internet users then covertly hack targets with third-party spyware. Unlike infections that rely on people interacting with links or files, the spyware requires no interaction from the victim to be installed, making it a new delivery technique, Citizen Lab says. The infections happen without a user’s knowledge, and in a matter of seconds, according to Citizen Lab. “[The online advertising] ecosystem is being weaponised at a massive scale to profile millions of users, then silently infect targets with zero-click mercenary spyware,” the report says. According to the report, Controlium is able to harvest a user’s identity and IP address when the user is shown a seemingly benign custom-created ad – for example, for a digital game or a telecoms service. If the user has been selected as a target for hacking, a mercenary spyware firm can then send a malicious code containing spyware to their device, the researchers say. They say that millions of users worldwide have been served ads by Discover-Tech since 2024, including in Yemen, Brazil, Mexico and Czechia. “It’s disastrous that major ad vendors and organisations apparently were neither able to detect nor prevent the company’s malicious advertising operations for years,” said Wolfie Christl, a researcher at Citizen Lab. “The way the online advertising ecosystem works today is a security threat for states, the private sector, civil society and everyone else alike.” According to Citizen Lab, Controlium acts as a “facilitator” for third-party spyware firms that have targeted “government officials, journalists, businesspeople, activists, academics and embassy workers”. Citizen Lab claims it can deliver spyware that can access everything on the device of a target, extracting messages, photos and emails, recording calls and secretly activating microphones. The full extent of the targeting allegedly enabled by Discover-Tech is unknown. Citizen Lab’s findings join mounting evidence that the opaque arrangements underpinning the world of online advertising can be leveraged for surveillance. “There has been a lot of buzz that online ads can be used to identify and automatically hack targets with pinpoint precision, but now for the first time, we have concrete technical evidence showing this process in action,” said Bill Marczak, a researcher at Citizen Lab. Discover-Tech has been approached for comment. These bids are based on the user’s profile, which can include information about their device and data compiled on them by tracking their activity across the web. For example, companies given the profile of a 35-year-old interested in sports betting and crypto might bid to show that individual an advertisement for an energy drink. There is little regulation on this automated online market, and there is growing evidence that it is being exploited by malevolent actors. Reuters has reported that billions of dollars’ worth of Meta’s ad revenue comes from ads for scams, illegal gambling, pornography and other banned content. In the US, ICE and other government agencies have bought software that uses ad tech data to track people’s movements. “Cybersecurity agencies, regulators and lawmakers in the US, Europe and other regions must urgently step in. They must investigate the involved companies and fix the systemic risks that enable malicious ad targeting,” said Christl.

extraction.body: Dubbing the attacks “AdFection,” the researchers documented a campaign in which an Israeli-registered advertising firm allegedly connected to the servers linked to a spyware company and infected dozens of devices with its invasive malware. Citizen Lab believes this to be the first detailed technical evidence made publicly available of sophisticated spyware infecting devices via digital ads. Zero-click hacks are a holy grail for attackers and catastrophic for victims, because they can automatically install malware on devices without requiring any interaction or missteps from the target. When sophisticated hackers have deployed rare zero-click attacks in recent years, they have often exploited vulnerabilities in mobile messaging and communication apps to infect victims. But attackers have also exploited the sprawling infrastructure of the online ad ecosystem to distribute malware, sometimes with little or no interaction needed from victims. Evidence of the zero-click spyware campaign that Citizen Lab’s researchers uncovered shows the two threats merging, underscoring the extent and urgency of the risk. “AdFection allows operators to automatically hack specific individuals with mercenary spyware as they use apps or browse the internet,” says Bill Marczak, a senior researcher at Citizen Lab. In fact, they might not even see any ad at all.” The situation is so concerning, he notes, because there isn’t much that people can do to protect themselves from zero-click ad attacks other than blocking ads as thoroughly as possible on all websites and platforms—a fact that intelligence agencies like the NSA and CIA seem to know all too well. “The risk of having your device infected with spyware simply by using a website or app that displays ads is a nightmare scenario,” says Wolfie Christl, a senior Citizen Lab researcher. During 2024 and 2025, Citizen Lab concluded that 45 devices belonging to the news outlet Al Jazeera were targeted with zero-click attacks delivered by ads. The researchers say that the targeted ads were issued by the Israeli-founded marketing firm Discover-Tech and distributed spyware attributed to the Israeli developer Candiru. Infected devices had contact with domains linked to Discover-Tech and then connected to infrastructure associated with Candiru, according to Citizen Lab’s analysis. (Al Jazeera, which participated in the investigation and shared device logs with Citizen Lab researchers, did not respond to a request for comment.) “The ability to push individualized, arbitrary content at specific users is a hallmark of the modern online ads ecosystem, and is perfectly suited to the mercenary spyware industry,” Marczak says. “Until this architecture changes, or ad companies get serious about customer vetting, we’re going to keep seeing this kind of abuse.” Emails and messages sent to Discover-Tech and its CEO by WIRED did not receive a response before publication. Google, which operates one of the world’s largest advertising businesses, terminated Discover-Tech’s registration after collaborating with Citizen Lab and researchers from the cybersecurity firm Confiant and confirming a spyware link. “Following a joint investigation with Citizen Lab and Confiant, Google blocked Discover-Tech from our ad platforms for systematically violating our policies,” a Google spokesperson says. “We also set up Safe Browsing warnings to help protect people if they navigate to websites linked to this group.” The European branch of the Interactive Advertising Bureau (IAB), an ad industry body, confirmed to WIRED that it has suspended Discover-Tech from its global vendor list, known as the GVL. The company was suspended by IAB Europe following an audit of its policies, it says. “Further confirmation of the findings regarding spyware could also justify a definitive expulsion from the GVL,” a spokesperson for IAB Europe says. A spokesperson for Beeswax, an online advertising industry company owned by Comcast, says in a statement: “Beeswax removed Discovery-Tech from our platform following recent activity and independent validation by a third-party security specialist. We maintain a zero-tolerance policy for malicious advertising.” Often when you see ads online or in apps, they’re displayed following a complex process known as real-time bidding—essentially an automated auction where advertisers place bids to show you specific ads. The process has been a privacy nightmare for years, with murky data brokers selling people’s personal information, and law enforcement agencies and hostile nations buying it to track or target people. The Citizen Lab researchers say that Discover-Tech operates an advertising platform, Controlium, that can allow its users to “de-anonymize, fingerprint, and automatically infect devices” once an ad appears. Overall, the researchers estimate that millions of devices were directed to Candiru’s servers, where they could be profiled. By analyzing ad-bidding records that were publicly exposed on the Discover-Tech website, the Citizen Lab researchers say, ads linked to the firm with attacker script tags were shown in more than 70,000 mobile apps and more than 120,000 websites between March and June this year. Multiple apps, the researchers say, displayed more than a million ads linked to Discover-Tech. The firm’s ads weren’t necessarily all weaponized to potentially distribute spyware, but the researchers say that, in general, they have seen Discover-Tech ad impressions on government and national-security-linked networks around the world. Previous zero-click targeted ad campaigns that distribute spyware have rarely surfaced publicly, but the Citizen Lab researchers say this is likely a symptom of ad infrastructure being so extensively trusted and incorporated in all aspects of digital life without specific oversight. “The network logs from Al Jazeera were key in understanding the ad-based nature of that attack,” Marczak says. “If a user’s personal device were targeted, say, while they were connected to their home Wi-Fi or mobile data, there’s not going to be the same level of network monitoring there. So I think the lack of prior reporting is probably mainly a visibility issue: Defenders have to be in the right place at the right time, looking at the right data.” Speaking generally about threats that can result from the sheer ubiquity of the digital ad ecosystem, Jason Kint, CEO of the digital media trade organization Digital Content Next (WIRED parent company Condé Nast is a member), says these kinds of attacks are both plausible and damaging. “Although rare and sophisticated, I wouldn’t be entirely surprised to learn about zero-click attacks through ads,” Kint says. “Anything that goes directly against users’ expectations or lowers the trust in the open web is deeply concerning.”

passages: Dunwoody’s struggle for balance between privacy and security is visible in other cities.
Some are shutting down their cameras and ripping them off lightpoles.

Last month amid an outcry, the city of Mountain View, California, shut off all of its Flock cameras after they discovered in an audit that federal agencies had accessed the city’s camera data without explicit local authorization in a brief period of 2024.
Jordan and a collection of security technologists have been looking closely at Flock Safety’s gear for months.

They are concerned about privacy issues, but have approached this as a hacking challenge to prove a point: surveillance technology with security vulnerabilities may do more harm than good when misused.
Dunwoody again postponed re-signing its Flock contract last Monday, citing community concerns about privacy.

A Dunwoody resident, Jason Hunyar, said that he discovered through records requests that a live feed from the Marcus Jewish Community Center of Atlanta had been shared through the Flock network, even though the center’s private network had been marked in the system as “do not share”.
Flock uses imagery data to train artificial intelligence.

In the wake of a Super Bowl ad highlighting Amazon’s Ring cameras use of AI to track down lost dogs, customers quickly understood the corollary: their cameras could be used to track people, too. , The ad provoked intense backlash, and precipitated an end to Ring’s partnership with Flock Safety.

The findings Jordan publicized in YouTube videos have either been fixed – like cameras that were misconfigured to stream video – or did not exist in properlyinstalled systems, like being able to access a camera through a diagnostic tool, Castaldo said.
The Miami-Dade county sheriff’s office recently tore some Flock cameras apart as a penetration test, looking for vulnerabilities and came back clean, Castaldo said.

“When you hear from our police department saying they trust Flock, it’s clear that our police are too lazy to verify what a vendor such as Flock says,” said Joe Hirsh, a Dunwoody resident, haranguing the council over privacy breaches last week.
“You and I both know the next time Flock is misused in our city, you will turn a blind eye because none of you are trustworthy with our records.”
“Let’s say I was a crazy abusive partner,” Jordan said.

“If she said, you know, ‘I went for a walk,’ and I said, ‘no, you got picked up and cheated on me,’ I could go to each Flock camera and do this and see if she’s on the local, because it does take pictures every time the radar sensor detects movement, then it will take that image and store it on the camera.”
Lautenbacher cited that video while talking with Flock’s public relations director at the Dunwoody hearing last month.
With more than 80,000 cameras in its network, that data sharing agreement makes Flock attractive for local investigators tracking crime suspects fleeing their jurisdiction.
But it also means other agencies can reach into a local police department’s records of license plate sightings looking for someone.
The debate has been loudest in California, which passed a law in 2015 barring municipalities from sharing automatic license plate data with federal or out-of-state agencies.
Flock disabled that function for California cities in March 2025, to comply with state law.

Jordan and security researchers Joshua Michael and Jon Gaines demonstrated how the hardware of one Flock camera they purchased from an online vendor could be penetrated simply by pushing the button on the front three times while using a common Android operating system diagnostic tool.
The password to the device was coded in the firmware and readable with the device.
With that password, they could upload, download or delete videos.
Still, among the videos which have millions of views on YouTube, one shows Jordan watching himself on his phone, streamed live from a Flock camera hanging above his head on a pole.
Jordan had found some of Flock’s Condor cameras were streaming their feeds live to the open internet, and that some of that archived footage was accessible.
404 Media revealed in May 2025 that local police around the country had repeatedly searched Flock’s database to assist federal immigration enforcement.

The system includes gunshot detection devices and M350 drones with Flock Aerodome software that police can deploy in 30 seconds from its headquarters to the mall or a street junction to provide aerial surveillance before police can get there in a car.
He describes this in one video as “Netflix for stalkers”.
They said they report all of their findings to Flock before posting anything.
The Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) strategy for immigration enforcement has increasingly relied on imagery-driven technology and data analysis.
The DHS entered a five-year, up to $1bn agreement with Palantir Technologies to build profiles of deportation targets, and has a contract with Clearview AI for facial recognition software.
Miami’s police use gunshot detection and other technology from Flock Safety, and appear to be happy with the tools.
Meanwhile, Flagstaff, Arizona, deactivated its cameras and then physically removed them.
Denver cancelled its contract with Flock and is preparing to sign a new contract with Axon to administer license plate readers.
Benn Jordan’s cluttered studio-slash-laboratory in the Atlanta suburbs has a synthesizer in one corner and computer chop-shop workbench in the other, befitting his general Buckaroo Banzai vibe.

extraction.body: Some cities are cutting ties with firm that provides license plate reader cameras, others are signing new contracts and many are still looking for their footing In recent city council meetings in Dunwoody, Georgia , a spokesman for Flock Safety, a Georgia-based firm that provides automated license plate readers, has found himself in the hot seat again. “When you hear from our police department saying they trust Flock, it’s clear that our police are too lazy to verify what a vendor such as Flock says,” said Joe Hirsh, a Dunwoody resident, haranguing the council over privacy breaches last week. “You and I both know the next time Flock is misused in our city, you will turn a blind eye because none of you are trustworthy with our records.” Kerry McCormack, Flock Group Inc’s public relations manager for the east coast, spent about half an hour explaining that the company doesn’t own the images its increasingly ubiquitous license plate reader cameras take, and that it doesn’t sell the data. “One hundred per cent of data, which is the photo of the public license plate, is owned by our customers,” McCormack said. “So, you own that data. It is never sold. We don’t have that in our model. It is written into your contract. We do not sell data.” Leaders in Dunwoody voted to defer renewal of its contract while its staff worked out the details with Flock. But they didn’t cancel the contract outright – not after investing $360,000 to build a real-time crime center and about half a million a year with Flock Safety in its technology and network. Dunwoody’s struggle for balance between privacy and security is visible in other cities. Some are shutting down their cameras and ripping them off lightpoles. Others are signing new contracts, albeit with stronger language about how data is shared. Many are still looking for their footing. Benn Jordan’s cluttered studio-slash-laboratory in the Atlanta suburbs has a synthesizer in one corner and computer chop-shop workbench in the other, befitting his general Buckaroo Banzai vibe. “I’m a scientist and YouTuber and musician,” he said. “I’m basically just somebody who asks a lot of questions about everything.” Jordan and a collection of security technologists have been looking closely at Flock Safety’s gear for months. They are concerned about privacy issues, but have approached this as a hacking challenge to prove a point: surveillance technology with security vulnerabilities may do more harm than good when misused. They have shared their findings with the company, and the federal government’s academic information security apparatus, and now with the world through a series of YouTube videos highlighting the vulnerabilities of the cameras. Jordan and security researchers Joshua Michael and Jon Gaines demonstrated how the hardware of one Flock camera they purchased from an online vendor could be penetrated simply by pushing the button on the front three times while using a common Android operating system diagnostic tool. The password to the device was coded in the firmware and readable with the device. They said they report all of their findings to Flock before posting anything. Flock’s response has been to say that a device that isn’t connected to the internet doesn’t have the same network security protections as one that does, and that their findings don’t amount to a significant security issue. Still, among the videos which have millions of views on YouTube, one shows Jordan watching himself on his phone, streamed live from a Flock camera hanging above his head on a pole. Jordan had found some of Flock’s Condor cameras were streaming their feeds live to the open internet, and that some of that archived footage was accessible. Lautenbacher cited that video while talking with Flock’s public relations director at the Dunwoody hearing last month. “He said he hacked your cameras. You said that never happened?” “Our systems, our data, our customers data has never been hacked,” McCormack answered. “We’re aware of one instance … we put this stuff out when we find out about it.” McCormack attributed it to an installation error that was fixed immediately. extraction.body: Today, I’m talking with Benn Jordan, musician, YouTuber, researcher, and investigative journalist. You might know Benn from those first two titles — he’s got a prolific discography of experimental music dating back decades. But in the last couple of years, he’s become a high-profile face in the creator and media spaces for his work investigating Flock Safety, the maker of automatic license plate readers and the software that powers them. Benn recently testified in front of Congress, at a hearing the Senate Judiciary Committee’s Subcommittee on Crime and Counterterrorism held, dedicated to Flock and other ALPR systems. You can sign up here. --- This has led to major fallout for Flock. Hundreds of cities, counties, and other local governments have begun canceling contracts, and Flock is now under investigation by Republican Sen. Last week, Reuters reported that Flock plans to cut about 18 percent of its workforce. So of course I wanted to dig into all of that with Benn, not just because he played a role in that, but because he’s also become in some ways the face of a new front in the broader debate about surveillance and privacy. A point you’ll hear Benn make is that he doesn’t actually hate Flock as a company — he thinks its posture toward critics has been a colossal PR failure that made it low-hanging fruit, while competitors like Axon and Motorola quietly build the same kind of networks. Instead, Benn now talks to Flock directly, including to its CEO Garrett Langley, and reports security vulnerabilities to the company when he finds them. (As a side note: we have also invited Flock’s CEO on the show; Garrett if you’re listening, we would love to have you.) Benn says his outreach to the company is an olive branch he’s extended to Flock as part of his goal of working toward real, tangible solutions to surveillance overreach, rather than part of a crusade to tear one single company down. That’s a real theme throughout our conversation: that Flock and other high profile names in surveillance are just part of the problem — our real focus should be on the interlocking relationship between private industry, government, and law enforcement that prioritizes secrecy over transparency. So Benn sees his work on YouTube and with other researchers, civil rights groups, and journalists as an accountability function that forces this conversation to the forefront. Okay: Benn Jordan on Flock, privacy, and the new surveillance backlash. Benn Jordan, you’re a musician, YouTuber, and researcher. A lot of people in the Verge audience know you as a musician, but lately you have been relentlessly focused on Flock cameras, which are automatic license-plate readers (ALPRs). You recently testified in front of a Senate hearing on those cameras and the surveillance they enable. For people who don’t know you or haven’t been following you for years, where did Benn Jordan come from and how did you end up being the person who makes videos about Flock? I’ve been a musician my entire life, pretty much. If I get a product that wants me to pay for a service that’s already in the product, then that’s a puzzle I want to solve and I get excited about it. With the Flock stuff, it’s just that I live in Atlanta, which has more Flock cameras than anywhere else per square mile. There’s a question that’s been rattling around my head the entire time we’ve been having what I would call the modern privacy and surveillance debate. The Apple Watch is going to start doing automatic transcriptions, and everyone said, “Wait, hold on. I can’t say, “I don’t want these Flock cameras or Axon cameras or whatever they are tracking my every move and giving it to law enforcement.” I have no option to do that. This is just my property taxes going up and I’m paying for surveillance. Flock went from a company that was selling cameras to everyone, and the idea that adding Flock cameras would increase the safety of your town went from all but assumed to, “Hold on, we all have a lot of questions,” and now this company is struggling a little bit. The best news out of anything that’s happened is that with both Flock and data centers, it’s two things that have made people actually look up who their mayor is and who their city council members are and show up to meetings and then get involved in those local politics. People are so dissatisfied with the surveillance policies of their local politicians that it looks like that they may have a new mayor as a result of it, who also comes with a bunch of other interesting and progressive ideas that would probably help the city a lot more than the current mayor has. The other part that discourages me a little bit, or the part that I find a little disappointing, is that Flock has become this buzzword, but a lot of people don’t look beyond that. I just heard in the race for governor in Georgia that the Democratic candidate yesterday talked about getting rid of Flock cameras and being anti-Flock, when this is somebody who as mayor of Atlanta welcomed Flock. You see a lot of that happening now, too, where they just say “Flock bad” and then they go sign an Axon contract or they put Verkada or Motorola cameras everywhere. In my research, Flock has been the low-hanging fruit, just because they were the loudest and most defensive, whereas every other company was just taking a step back and cashing the checks. One of the pieces of the puzzle here that is just fascinating is that Flock is a startup, essentially. They’re a new company, they have a new go-to-market strategy. There’s something about Flock where Garrett Langley, the CEO, had a personality. There’s something about surveillance in that case where that strategy didn’t work. We just ran a big piece about the people of Utah pushing back on Kevin O’Leary, who called them all Chinese agents, and they were like, “What are you talking about?” That cut across party lines.

sources.title: This YouTuber Got Kicked Out of the Flock Convention. So He Ran His Own Surveillance. - Reason Magazine
passages: Although he hasn't gotten any response for his surveillance of the Flock conference, Jordan tells Reason that he's had police show up outside his house "and just blast their siren" in the past.

The surveillance contractor Flock Safety argues that police customers don't need a warrant to track drivers with its automated license plate reading cameras because drivers have "no reasonable expectation of privacy" on public roads.
So YouTube host Benn Jordan applied the same logic back on Flock.
He sat outside Flock's recent police convention in Atlanta with radio equipment and a drone, which he used to unmask attendees and even listen to microphones inside the convention hall.

Jordan, an early and outspoken critic of Flock, wanted to visit the convention to see what the relationship between police and the company was like after a string of cases in Georgia involving police misusing Flock products, he tells Reason .
Indeed, Jordan is careful not to reveal anything he picked up from his radio surveillance, telling Reason that the point was simply to show that it could be done.
Celebrate your independence with a subscription to Reason magazine, your most trusted source of honest, insightful news and analysis.
At least 56 cities and towns have ended their Flock contracts in 2026 over privacy concerns.
Ring, a doorbell camera company owned by Amazon, also canceled its planned partnership with Flock over public backlash.
Jordan, whose YouTube channel covers eclectic science topics from animal hearing to modern train synthesizers , accidentally found himself at the forefront of the movement against Flock.

In response to Jordan's video, Flock CEO Garrett Langley sent officials around the country a letter in December 2025 claiming that "Flock has never been hacked" and is "under coordinated attack…from the same activist groups who want to defund the police, weaken public safety, and normalize lawlessness." The city of Staunton, Virginia, published the letter in its announcement that it was ending its relationship with Flock.

Although automatic license plate readers have been raising privacy concerns for years, the growth of Flock is particularly alarming because the company plugs police departments around the country into a central database that isn't subject to court orders or the Fourth Amendment to the Constitution.
Ironically, government regulations helped Jordan with his surveillance, because the Federal Communications Commission limits wireless microphones to broadcast on very specific frequencies.

extraction.body: The surveillance contractor Flock Safety argues that police customers don't need a warrant to track drivers with its automated license plate reading cameras because drivers have "no reasonable expectation of privacy" on public roads. So YouTube host Benn Jordan applied the same logic back on Flock. He sat outside Flock's recent police convention in Atlanta with radio equipment and a drone, which he used to unmask attendees and even listen to microphones inside the convention hall. "Flock values their privacy. Oh well," Jordan wrote in the title of his video on the convention. His plans didn't quite start out that way. Jordan, an early and outspoken critic of Flock, wanted to visit the convention to see what the relationship between police and the company was like after a string of cases in Georgia involving police misusing Flock products, he tells Reason . After downloading the conference app, he looked inside the source code and found that it revealed the entire guest list. Jordan alerted Flock to the data breach. Once the company caught wind that Jordan was coming, it canceled his tickets. But the attempts to keep Jordan out went further than that. An employee from Flock called the hotel to cancel Jordan's room reservation, which he had booked himself, according to a video Jordan posted of a call with the hotel. (Flock did not respond to Reason 's request for comment.) Jordan even found out that all of the rest of the rooms and even the parking lots surrounding the hotel had been booked. Still, he was able to find a public parking spot within view of the hotel, where he parked a van with dozens of WiFi adapters, a parabolic dish antenna, and a dipole array. This equipment picked up the signal from the convention hall's wireless microphones, allowing Jordan to hear attendees' conversations. "Everything was on public channels," he says. Then he used a drone to photograph attendees walking out and used facial recognition to figure out their identities. Ironically, government regulations helped Jordan with his surveillance, because the Federal Communications Commission limits wireless microphones to broadcast on very specific frequencies. Although it's within a private company's right to choose who can and can't come to its conference—and Jordan acknowledges that keeping outsiders away from the hotel can be a reasonable security measure—many of the attendees were police officials, presumably attending on the taxpayer dime. More fundamentally, it's an issue of different rights for different people. While Flock and its police customers are happy to erode the expectation of privacy in everyday life, they carve out ultra-private spaces for themselves. Indeed, Jordan is careful not to reveal anything he picked up from his radio surveillance, telling Reason that the point was simply to show that it could be done. "Public officials should know that you can't go to a private thing where journalists aren't allowed and not expect anybody to fly a drone from public view. You should be a little unsettled about going to something like that," Jordan adds. He says that he's ultimately happy that his stunt drew attention to the lack of transparency. Although automatic license plate readers have been raising privacy concerns for years, the growth of Flock is particularly alarming because the company plugs police departments around the country into a central database that isn't subject to court orders or the Fourth Amendment to the Constitution. And the lack of oversight isn't just theoretical. Police officers have been caught using Flock data to stalk romantic interests . One woman spent two weeks in jail, and another was detained at gunpoint because of mistaken identifications from Flock cameras. The American public is becoming increasingly hostile to these cameras. At least 56 cities and towns have ended their Flock contracts in 2026 over privacy concerns. Ring, a doorbell camera company owned by Amazon, also canceled its planned partnership with Flock over public backlash. More alarmingly, citizens have started vandalizing the cameras . Jordan, whose YouTube channel covers eclectic science topics from animal hearing to modern train synthesizers , accidentally found himself at the forefront of the movement against Flock. He saw mysterious new cameras in his neighborhood early last year, followed his instincts to reverse engineer everything, and found security vulnerabilities allowing anyone to access Flock footage without a password. In response to Jordan's video, Flock CEO Garrett Langley sent officials around the country a letter in December 2025 claiming that "Flock has never been hacked" and is "under coordinated attack…from the same activist groups who want to defund the police, weaken public safety, and normalize lawlessness." The city of Staunton, Virginia, published the letter in its announcement that it was ending its relationship with Flock. Although he hasn't gotten any response for his surveillance of the Flock conference, Jordan tells Reason that he's had police show up outside his house "and just blast their siren" in the past. He claims he also spotted a private investigator (who is unlicensed and a convicted felon) hanging around his house, but couldn't figure out who hired them. Despite the unwanted attention, Jordan has continued speaking to city councils and police departments around the country. While he says that he would prefer no license plate tracking to begin with, he has been pitching a solution to cities that are going to do it anyway: locally owned cameras feeding into locally owned databases that police need a warrant from a judge to access. "I want there to be an end to this investigation…I generally never make a video about the same thing twice," Jordan tells Reason . "But unfortunately, I have cameras everywhere all around my neighborhood, so I can't not think about it." Start your day with Reason . Get a daily brief of the most important stories and trends every weekday morning when you subscribe to Reason Roundup . NEXT: Trump Threatens U.S. Relationship With Canada as Trade Talks Collapse Matthew Petti is an assistant editor at Reason . Celebrate your independence with a subscription to Reason magazine, your most trusted source of honest, insightful news and analysis. Williams, the longtime chief in Staunton, a town of about 25,000 in the Shenandoah Valley where Flock installed six license plate reading cameras in 2024, rejected Langley’s assertion that law enforcement is under attack. “What we are seeing here is a group of local citizens who are raising concerns that we could be potentially surveilling private citizens, residents and visitors and using the data for nefarious purposes,” Williams wrote to Langley. “In short,” he said, “it is democracy in action.” Video spurs scrutiny More than 80,000 Flock cameras are said to be in use throughout the U.S. Flock’s customers include an estimated 5,000 law enforcement agencies and 1,000 corporations. After Williams met with the city manager and city council to discuss Langley’s remarks, they decided to end the contract with Flock. Last month, Staunton joined the growing list of cities that are canceling contracts with Flock, amid a growing public backlash over the surveillance technology’s expansion.

City council meetings from Washington state to Massachusetts have been filled with concerned residents, many of whom accuse their local officials of entering into contracts that allow unwarranted spying without their input or knowledge.

Williams, the longtime chief in Staunton, a town of about 25,000 in the Shenandoah Valley where Flock installed six license plate reading cameras in 2024, rejected Langley’s assertion that law enforcement is under attack.

“What we are seeing here is a group of local citizens who are raising concerns that we could be potentially surveilling private citizens, residents and visitors and using the data for nefarious purposes,” Williams wrote to Langley.
“In short,” he said, “it is democracy in action.” Video spurs scrutiny More than 80,000 Flock cameras are said to be in use throughout the U.S.
Flock’s customers include an estimated 5,000 law enforcement agencies and 1,000 corporations.
Scrutiny of the company has intensified since a YouTube video revealed how live feeds from more than 60 cameras were exposed to the open internet.
Its producer, technologist Benn Jordan, told Straight Arrow News that he sent an email thanking Williams for what he saw as a rational response to Flock’s CEO.
Jordan also expressed concern over Langley’s email, which he believes may have been sent out en masse.

“I realized that Garrett Langley's original email was unsolicited and impersonal, coming from a ‘no_reply’ address, which suggests that this kind of message is going out to large amounts of law enforcement agencies around the country,” Jordan said.

“Intentionally misleading law enforcement and trying to get them to ‘join the fight’ against people critical of your company is incredibly reckless and dangerous.” “I've already had police show up to my house after taking video footage of Flock Safety cameras,” Jordan continued.

“How will they approach my house if they have reason to believe that I'm part of a ‘lawless coordinated attack’ on them?” SAN reached out to Flock with specific questions about Langley’s email and the contract cancellation in Staunton.
The company replied only with a link to a page on its website outlining its privacy and ethics guidelines.
A clash of values In Staunton, Williams said the Flock cameras had helped officers locate missing and wanted persons, recover stolen vehicles and identify suspects in crimes.
After Williams met with the city manager and city council to discuss Langley’s remarks, they decided to end the contract with Flock.
In a statement, the city said that Langley’s “narrative does not reflect” Staunton’s values.
“The Staunton Police Department reported numerous successes utilizing this technology,” the statement said.

“Unfortunately, the city does not agree with the assessment as detailed by the CEO of Flock Safety.” The city says it is currently coordinating with Flock to finalize the contract’s termination and to turn off and remove all license plate reading cameras. ‘A new era' The situation in Staunton is similar to a growing number of others, including in Flagstaff, Arizona, which terminated its contract with Flock in December after a month of pushback from local residents.
Despite efforts by police to ease concerns by outlining policy guardrails, the Flagstaff City Council ultimately voted unanimously to end the partnership.
Jan Carlile, a local resident who supported terminating the contract, said during public comment that the potential privacy ramifications were too much to bear.

“I admire and respect the efforts of our police department to try to do the very best they can to protect our safety, and until the advancement of AI and frankly the troubling efforts by our current national administration, both of those can potentially very seriously undercut our privacy as citizens," Carlile said.

"I would not likely have been concerned about the use of cameras as a tool for public safety [in the past], but we are in a new era.” Cambridge, Massachusetts, initially paused the use of 16 cameras in October.
But city officials canceled their contract entirely after it was revealed that Flock had installed two additional cameras without the city’s knowledge.
“Concerns about Flock were substantiated,” said city spokesperson Jeremy Warnick.
“Due to this material breach of our trust and the agreement, the city terminated its contract with Flock Safety.” In Evanston, Illinois, a similar series of events unfolded.
After the city terminated its contract in late August and deactivated 19 cameras, Flock began reinstalling cameras across the city, seemingly unbeknownst to local officials and residents.
The city responded in September by issuing a cease-and-desist order against Flock, which said that it would uninstall the cameras.
The controversy came around the same time that an audit by the Illinois Secretary of State found that Flock had violated state law by allowing U.S.
Washington state has also been a hotbed for backlash against Flock.
The cities of Redmond and Lynwood deactivated their cameras in November while reevaluating their contracts after complaints from residents.
The City Council in Mountlake Terrace unanimously canceled its contract in November, while the capital city of Olympia uninstalled 15 cameras and canceled its pilot program with Flock in December.

coreStoryFacts.text: Dunwoody’s struggle for balance between privacy and security is visible in other cities.
Some are shutting down their cameras and ripping them off lightpoles.

Last month amid an outcry, the city of Mountain View, California, shut off all of its Flock cameras after they discovered in an audit that federal agencies had accessed the city’s camera data without explicit local authorization in a brief period of 2024.
Jordan and a collection of security technologists have been looking closely at Flock Safety’s gear for months.

They are concerned about privacy issues, but have approached this as a hacking challenge to prove a point: surveillance technology with security vulnerabilities may do more harm than good when misused.
Dunwoody again postponed re-signing its Flock contract last Monday, citing community concerns about privacy.

A Dunwoody resident, Jason Hunyar, said that he discovered through records requests that a live feed from the Marcus Jewish Community Center of Atlanta had been shared through the Flock network, even though the center’s private network had been marked in the system as “do not share”.
Flock uses imagery data to train artificial intelligence.

In the wake of a Super Bowl ad highlighting Amazon’s Ring cameras use of AI to track down lost dogs, customers quickly understood the corollary: their cameras could be used to track people, too. , The ad provoked intense backlash, and precipitated an end to Ring’s partnership with Flock Safety.

The findings Jordan publicized in YouTube videos have either been fixed – like cameras that were misconfigured to stream video – or did not exist in properlyinstalled systems, like being able to access a camera through a diagnostic tool, Castaldo said.
The Miami-Dade county sheriff’s office recently tore some Flock cameras apart as a penetration test, looking for vulnerabilities and came back clean, Castaldo said.

“When you hear from our police department saying they trust Flock, it’s clear that our police are too lazy to verify what a vendor such as Flock says,” said Joe Hirsh, a Dunwoody resident, haranguing the council over privacy breaches last week.
“You and I both know the next time Flock is misused in our city, you will turn a blind eye because none of you are trustworthy with our records.”
“Let’s say I was a crazy abusive partner,” Jordan said.

“If she said, you know, ‘I went for a walk,’ and I said, ‘no, you got picked up and cheated on me,’ I could go to each Flock camera and do this and see if she’s on the local, because it does take pictures every time the radar sensor detects movement, then it will take that image and store it on the camera.”
Lautenbacher cited that video while talking with Flock’s public relations director at the Dunwoody hearing last month.
With more than 80,000 cameras in its network, that data sharing agreement makes Flock attractive for local investigators tracking crime suspects fleeing their jurisdiction.
But it also means other agencies can reach into a local police department’s records of license plate sightings looking for someone.
The debate has been loudest in California, which passed a law in 2015 barring municipalities from sharing automatic license plate data with federal or out-of-state agencies.
Flock disabled that function for California cities in March 2025, to comply with state law.

Jordan and security researchers Joshua Michael and Jon Gaines demonstrated how the hardware of one Flock camera they purchased from an online vendor could be penetrated simply by pushing the button on the front three times while using a common Android operating system diagnostic tool.
The password to the device was coded in the firmware and readable with the device.
With that password, they could upload, download or delete videos.
Still, among the videos which have millions of views on YouTube, one shows Jordan watching himself on his phone, streamed live from a Flock camera hanging above his head on a pole.

extraction.body: Some cities are cutting ties with firm that provides license plate reader cameras, others are signing new contracts and many are still looking for their footing In recent city council meetings in Dunwoody, Georgia , a spokesman for Flock Safety, a Georgia-based firm that provides automated license plate readers, has found himself in the hot seat again. “When you hear from our police department saying they trust Flock, it’s clear that our police are too lazy to verify what a vendor such as Flock says,” said Joe Hirsh, a Dunwoody resident, haranguing the council over privacy breaches last week. “You and I both know the next time Flock is misused in our city, you will turn a blind eye because none of you are trustworthy with our records.” Kerry McCormack, Flock Group Inc’s public relations manager for the east coast, spent about half an hour explaining that the company doesn’t own the images its increasingly ubiquitous license plate reader cameras take, and that it doesn’t sell the data. “One hundred per cent of data, which is the photo of the public license plate, is owned by our customers,” McCormack said. “So, you own that data. It is never sold. We don’t have that in our model. It is written into your contract. We do not sell data.” Leaders in Dunwoody voted to defer renewal of its contract while its staff worked out the details with Flock. But they didn’t cancel the contract outright – not after investing $360,000 to build a real-time crime center and about half a million a year with Flock Safety in its technology and network. Dunwoody’s struggle for balance between privacy and security is visible in other cities. Some are shutting down their cameras and ripping them off lightpoles. Others are signing new contracts, albeit with stronger language about how data is shared. Many are still looking for their footing. Benn Jordan’s cluttered studio-slash-laboratory in the Atlanta suburbs has a synthesizer in one corner and computer chop-shop workbench in the other, befitting his general Buckaroo Banzai vibe. “I’m a scientist and YouTuber and musician,” he said. “I’m basically just somebody who asks a lot of questions about everything.” Jordan and a collection of security technologists have been looking closely at Flock Safety’s gear for months. They are concerned about privacy issues, but have approached this as a hacking challenge to prove a point: surveillance technology with security vulnerabilities may do more harm than good when misused. They have shared their findings with the company, and the federal government’s academic information security apparatus, and now with the world through a series of YouTube videos highlighting the vulnerabilities of the cameras. Jordan and security researchers Joshua Michael and Jon Gaines demonstrated how the hardware of one Flock camera they purchased from an online vendor could be penetrated simply by pushing the button on the front three times while using a common Android operating system diagnostic tool. The password to the device was coded in the firmware and readable with the device. With that password, they could upload, download or delete videos. “Let’s say I was a crazy abusive partner,” Jordan said. “If she said, you know, ‘I went for a walk,’ and I said, ‘no, you got picked up and cheated on me,’ I could go to each Flock camera and do this and see if she’s on the local, because it does take pictures every time the radar sensor detects movement, then it will take that image and store it on the camera.” He describes this in one video as “Netflix for stalkers”. They said they report all of their findings to Flock before posting anything. Flock’s response has been to say that a device that isn’t connected to the internet doesn’t have the same network security protections as one that does, and that their findings don’t amount to a significant security issue. Still, among the videos which have millions of views on YouTube, one shows Jordan watching himself on his phone, streamed live from a Flock camera hanging above his head on a pole. Jordan had found some of Flock’s Condor cameras were streaming their feeds live to the open internet, and that some of that archived footage was accessible. Lautenbacher cited that video while talking with Flock’s public relations director at the Dunwoody hearing last month. “He said he hacked your cameras. You said that never happened?” “Our systems, our data, our customers data has never been hacked,” McCormack answered. “We’re aware of one instance … we put this stuff out when we find out about it.” McCormack attributed it to an installation error that was fixed immediately. Though other companies make automated license plate readers, Flock Safety may be in the headlines because it offers its police customers a unique service: nationwide search capacity. extraction.body: Today, I’m talking with Benn Jordan, musician, YouTuber, researcher, and investigative journalist. You might know Benn from those first two titles — he’s got a prolific discography of experimental music dating back decades. But in the last couple of years, he’s become a high-profile face in the creator and media spaces for his work investigating Flock Safety, the maker of automatic license plate readers and the software that powers them. Benn recently testified in front of Congress, at a hearing the Senate Judiciary Committee’s Subcommittee on Crime and Counterterrorism held, dedicated to Flock and other ALPR systems. You can sign up here. --- This has led to major fallout for Flock. Hundreds of cities, counties, and other local governments have begun canceling contracts, and Flock is now under investigation by Republican Sen. Last week, Reuters reported that Flock plans to cut about 18 percent of its workforce. So of course I wanted to dig into all of that with Benn, not just because he played a role in that, but because he’s also become in some ways the face of a new front in the broader debate about surveillance and privacy. A point you’ll hear Benn make is that he doesn’t actually hate Flock as a company — he thinks its posture toward critics has been a colossal PR failure that made it low-hanging fruit, while competitors like Axon and Motorola quietly build the same kind of networks. Instead, Benn now talks to Flock directly, including to its CEO Garrett Langley, and reports security vulnerabilities to the company when he finds them. (As a side note: we have also invited Flock’s CEO on the show; Garrett if you’re listening, we would love to have you.) Benn says his outreach to the company is an olive branch he’s extended to Flock as part of his goal of working toward real, tangible solutions to surveillance overreach, rather than part of a crusade to tear one single company down. That’s a real theme throughout our conversation: that Flock and other high profile names in surveillance are just part of the problem — our real focus should be on the interlocking relationship between private industry, government, and law enforcement that prioritizes secrecy over transparency. So Benn sees his work on YouTube and with other researchers, civil rights groups, and journalists as an accountability function that forces this conversation to the forefront. Okay: Benn Jordan on Flock, privacy, and the new surveillance backlash. Benn Jordan, you’re a musician, YouTuber, and researcher. A lot of people in the Verge audience know you as a musician, but lately you have been relentlessly focused on Flock cameras, which are automatic license-plate readers (ALPRs). You recently testified in front of a Senate hearing on those cameras and the surveillance they enable. For people who don’t know you or haven’t been following you for years, where did Benn Jordan come from and how did you end up being the person who makes videos about Flock? I’ve been a musician my entire life, pretty much. If I get a product that wants me to pay for a service that’s already in the product, then that’s a puzzle I want to solve and I get excited about it. With the Flock stuff, it’s just that I live in Atlanta, which has more Flock cameras than anywhere else per square mile. There’s a question that’s been rattling around my head the entire time we’ve been having what I would call the modern privacy and surveillance debate. The Apple Watch is going to start doing automatic transcriptions, and everyone said, “Wait, hold on. I can’t say, “I don’t want these Flock cameras or Axon cameras or whatever they are tracking my every move and giving it to law enforcement.” I have no option to do that. This is just my property taxes going up and I’m paying for surveillance. Flock went from a company that was selling cameras to everyone, and the idea that adding Flock cameras would increase the safety of your town went from all but assumed to, “Hold on, we all have a lot of questions,” and now this company is struggling a little bit. The best news out of anything that’s happened is that with both Flock and data centers, it’s two things that have made people actually look up who their mayor is and who their city council members are and show up to meetings and then get involved in those local politics. People are so dissatisfied with the surveillance policies of their local politicians that it looks like that they may have a new mayor as a result of it, who also comes with a bunch of other interesting and progressive ideas that would probably help the city a lot more than the current mayor has. The other part that discourages me a little bit, or the part that I find a little disappointing, is that Flock has become this buzzword, but a lot of people don’t look beyond that. I just heard in the race for governor in Georgia that the Democratic candidate yesterday talked about getting rid of Flock cameras and being anti-Flock, when this is somebody who as mayor of Atlanta welcomed Flock. You see a lot of that happening now, too, where they just say “Flock bad” and then they go sign an Axon contract or they put Verkada or Motorola cameras everywhere. In my research, Flock has been the low-hanging fruit, just because they were the loudest and most defensive, whereas every other company was just taking a step back and cashing the checks. One of the pieces of the puzzle here that is just fascinating is that Flock is a startup, essentially. They’re a new company, they have a new go-to-market strategy. There’s something about Flock where Garrett Langley, the CEO, had a personality. There’s something about surveillance in that case where that strategy didn’t work. We just ran a big piece about the people of Utah pushing back on Kevin O’Leary, who called them all Chinese agents, and they were like, “What are you talking about?” That cut across party lines.

sources.title: This YouTuber Got Kicked Out of the Flock Convention. So He Ran His Own Surveillance. - Reason Magazine
passages: Although he hasn't gotten any response for his surveillance of the Flock conference, Jordan tells Reason that he's had police show up outside his house "and just blast their siren" in the past.

The surveillance contractor Flock Safety argues that police customers don't need a warrant to track drivers with its automated license plate reading cameras because drivers have "no reasonable expectation of privacy" on public roads.
So YouTube host Benn Jordan applied the same logic back on Flock.
He sat outside Flock's recent police convention in Atlanta with radio equipment and a drone, which he used to unmask attendees and even listen to microphones inside the convention hall.

Jordan, an early and outspoken critic of Flock, wanted to visit the convention to see what the relationship between police and the company was like after a string of cases in Georgia involving police misusing Flock products, he tells Reason .
Indeed, Jordan is careful not to reveal anything he picked up from his radio surveillance, telling Reason that the point was simply to show that it could be done.
Celebrate your independence with a subscription to Reason magazine, your most trusted source of honest, insightful news and analysis.
At least 56 cities and towns have ended their Flock contracts in 2026 over privacy concerns.
Ring, a doorbell camera company owned by Amazon, also canceled its planned partnership with Flock over public backlash.
Jordan, whose YouTube channel covers eclectic science topics from animal hearing to modern train synthesizers , accidentally found himself at the forefront of the movement against Flock.

In response to Jordan's video, Flock CEO Garrett Langley sent officials around the country a letter in December 2025 claiming that "Flock has never been hacked" and is "under coordinated attack…from the same activist groups who want to defund the police, weaken public safety, and normalize lawlessness." The city of Staunton, Virginia, published the letter in its announcement that it was ending its relationship with Flock.

Although automatic license plate readers have been raising privacy concerns for years, the growth of Flock is particularly alarming because the company plugs police departments around the country into a central database that isn't subject to court orders or the Fourth Amendment to the Constitution.
Ironically, government regulations helped Jordan with his surveillance, because the Federal Communications Commission limits wireless microphones to broadcast on very specific frequencies.
