extraction.body: The surveillance contractor Flock Safety argues that police customers don't need a warrant to track drivers with its automated license plate reading cameras because drivers have "no reasonable expectation of privacy" on public roads. So YouTube host Benn Jordan applied the same logic back on Flock. He sat outside Flock's recent police convention in Atlanta with radio equipment and a drone, which he used to unmask attendees and even listen to microphones inside the convention hall. "Flock values their privacy. Oh well," Jordan wrote in the title of his video on the convention. His plans didn't quite start out that way. Jordan, an early and outspoken critic of Flock, wanted to visit the convention to see what the relationship between police and the company was like after a string of cases in Georgia involving police misusing Flock products, he tells Reason . After downloading the conference app, he looked inside the source code and found that it revealed the entire guest list. Jordan alerted Flock to the data breach. Once the company caught wind that Jordan was coming, it canceled his tickets. But the attempts to keep Jordan out went further than that. An employee from Flock called the hotel to cancel Jordan's room reservation, which he had booked himself, according to a video Jordan posted of a call with the hotel. (Flock did not respond to Reason 's request for comment.) Jordan even found out that all of the rest of the rooms and even the parking lots surrounding the hotel had been booked. Still, he was able to find a public parking spot within view of the hotel, where he parked a van with dozens of WiFi adapters, a parabolic dish antenna, and a dipole array. This equipment picked up the signal from the convention hall's wireless microphones, allowing Jordan to hear attendees' conversations. "Everything was on public channels," he says. Then he used a drone to photograph attendees walking out and used facial recognition to figure out their identities. Ironically, government regulations helped Jordan with his surveillance, because the Federal Communications Commission limits wireless microphones to broadcast on very specific frequencies. Although it's within a private company's right to choose who can and can't come to its conference—and Jordan acknowledges that keeping outsiders away from the hotel can be a reasonable security measure—many of the attendees were police officials, presumably attending on the taxpayer dime. More fundamentally, it's an issue of different rights for different people. While Flock and its police customers are happy to erode the expectation of privacy in everyday life, they carve out ultra-private spaces for themselves. Indeed, Jordan is careful not to reveal anything he picked up from his radio surveillance, telling Reason that the point was simply to show that it could be done. "Public officials should know that you can't go to a private thing where journalists aren't allowed and not expect anybody to fly a drone from public view. You should be a little unsettled about going to something like that," Jordan adds. He says that he's ultimately happy that his stunt drew attention to the lack of transparency. Although automatic license plate readers have been raising privacy concerns for years, the growth of Flock is particularly alarming because the company plugs police departments around the country into a central database that isn't subject to court orders or the Fourth Amendment to the Constitution. And the lack of oversight isn't just theoretical. Police officers have been caught using Flock data to stalk romantic interests . One woman spent two weeks in jail, and another was detained at gunpoint because of mistaken identifications from Flock cameras. The American public is becoming increasingly hostile to these cameras. At least 56 cities and towns have ended their Flock contracts in 2026 over privacy concerns. Ring, a doorbell camera company owned by Amazon, also canceled its planned partnership with Flock over public backlash. More alarmingly, citizens have started vandalizing the cameras . Jordan, whose YouTube channel covers eclectic science topics from animal hearing to modern train synthesizers , accidentally found himself at the forefront of the movement against Flock. He saw mysterious new cameras in his neighborhood early last year, followed his instincts to reverse engineer everything, and found security vulnerabilities allowing anyone to access Flock footage without a password. In response to Jordan's video, Flock CEO Garrett Langley sent officials around the country a letter in December 2025 claiming that "Flock has never been hacked" and is "under coordinated attack…from the same activist groups who want to defund the police, weaken public safety, and normalize lawlessness." The city of Staunton, Virginia, published the letter in its announcement that it was ending its relationship with Flock. Although he hasn't gotten any response for his surveillance of the Flock conference, Jordan tells Reason that he's had police show up outside his house "and just blast their siren" in the past. He claims he also spotted a private investigator (who is unlicensed and a convicted felon) hanging around his house, but couldn't figure out who hired them. Despite the unwanted attention, Jordan has continued speaking to city councils and police departments around the country. While he says that he would prefer no license plate tracking to begin with, he has been pitching a solution to cities that are going to do it anyway: locally owned cameras feeding into locally owned databases that police need a warrant from a judge to access. "I want there to be an end to this investigation…I generally never make a video about the same thing twice," Jordan tells Reason . "But unfortunately, I have cameras everywhere all around my neighborhood, so I can't not think about it." Start your day with Reason . Get a daily brief of the most important stories and trends every weekday morning when you subscribe to Reason Roundup . NEXT: Trump Threatens U.S. Relationship With Canada as Trade Talks Collapse Matthew Petti is an assistant editor at Reason . Celebrate your independence with a subscription to Reason magazine, your most trusted source of honest, insightful news and analysis. Last month, Staunton joined the growing list of cities that are canceling contracts with Flock, amid a growing public backlash over the surveillance technology’s expansion.

City council meetings from Washington state to Massachusetts have been filled with concerned residents, many of whom accuse their local officials of entering into contracts that allow unwarranted spying without their input or knowledge.

Williams, the longtime chief in Staunton, a town of about 25,000 in the Shenandoah Valley where Flock installed six license plate reading cameras in 2024, rejected Langley’s assertion that law enforcement is under attack.

“What we are seeing here is a group of local citizens who are raising concerns that we could be potentially surveilling private citizens, residents and visitors and using the data for nefarious purposes,” Williams wrote to Langley.
“In short,” he said, “it is democracy in action.” Video spurs scrutiny More than 80,000 Flock cameras are said to be in use throughout the U.S.

The company replied only with a link to a page on its website outlining its privacy and ethics guidelines.

passages: The Chinese social media company is in advanced talks with MediaTek over the supply of bespoke chips that will help run ByteDance data centers, people familiar with the matter said.

The Taiwanese firm will provide an unspecified amount of Application Specific Integrated Circuits, or chips customized to work with a clients' platform, the people said, asking to remain anonymous to talk about a private arrangement.
If the deal goes through, ByteDance may become MediaTek's second major customer for such ASICs, after Alphabet Inc.'s Google.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.

China's biggest private firm is thus exploring alternatives including partnerships with chip designers — something that's allowed under current US export curbs so long as the AI computing power a Chinese firm is seeking doesn't exceed a certain threshold.
ByteDance struck a similar deal with Qualcomm earlier this year to procure millions of AI chips, Bloomberg News reported.

(Bloomberg) -- ByteDance Ltd. is close to an agreement to buy MediaTek Inc. data center semiconductors, a deal that would secure vital components for TikTok's owner while helping the Taiwanese chipmaker compete with Qualcomm Inc.
ByteDance is ramping up hardware spending to fuel a bet on AI as its next growth engine.
But like Chinese rivals Alibaba Group Holding Ltd. and Tencent Holdings Ltd., it's barred from the most cutting-edge AI chips from the likes of Nvidia Corp.
Local players such as Huawei Technologies Co. can't meet all demand.
ByteDance didn't have immediate comment, while MediaTek representatives declined to comment.

Like the largest US firms, ByteDance and its Chinese rivals plan to ramp up spending on the infrastructure required to train and run AI services — in anticipation of widespread consumer adoption as the technology evolves.

MediaTek has emerged as a key beneficiary of a push by technology companies to design custom semiconductors for AI applications, using its expertise in mobile processors to participate in the data center infrastructure rush.
ByteDance's spending marks a new, much more aggressive push to cement an early lead in key segments like chatbots and video, and expand its influence overseas.

passages: ByteDance, the company behind TikTok and Seedance, is close to an agreement with MediaTek to secure custom AI chips for its data centers operations, Bloomberg reported, citing people familiar with the matter.
This aggrement would help TikTok’s owner secure advanced AI chips, while MediaTek would see it as a major push towards expanding beyond mobile processors.
The Chinese firm struck a similar deal with Qualcomm earlier this year to procure millions of AI chips, per Bloomberg.
ByteDance is betting big on AI and is therefore considering boosting its spending up to $70 billion on data centers and AI infrastructure, which is more than double of last year’s total.
The company had secured a $30 billion load in September to fund its AI growth.
ByteDance, like any other big tech giant right now, is putting a lot of money into hardware spending as it bets AI as its next big growth engine.

The Taiwanese firm will reportedly provide Application Specific Integrated Circuits (ASICs) or chips customized to work with a client’s platform, although the volume of the discussion has not been disclosed.
If it goes through, which seems likely to be happening, ByteDance may become MediaTek’s second major customer for such ASICs after Google.
This deal would also mean a huge win for the Taiwanese chip giant and a big push to its efforts to diversify away from mobile processors and compete with Qualcomm and Broadcom in data centers.
ByteDance and MediaTek have yet to officially confirm anything on this matter.
With talks nearing the final stages, we expect an official confirmation soon, if everything remains favourable.

The Chinese social media company is in advanced talks with MediaTek over the supply of bespoke chips that will help run ByteDance data centers, people familiar with the matter said. The Taiwanese firm will provide an unspecified amount of Application Specific Integrated Circuits, or chips customized to work with a clients' platform, the people said, asking to remain anonymous to talk about a private arrangement. If the deal goes through, ByteDance may become MediaTek's second major customer for such ASICs, after Alphabet Inc.'s Google.

ByteDance is ramping up hardware spending to fuel a bet on AI as its next growth engine. Local players such as Huawei Technologies Co. can't meet all demand.

For MediaTek, a large-scale contract win would boost its efforts to diversify away from mobile phones and compete with Qualcomm and Broadcom Inc. in data centers, an arena it's less familiar with. ByteDance represents an opportunity for MediaTek: a high-volume customer that should galvanize the Taiwanese firm's foray into one of the fastest-growing segments of the semiconductor industry. That may rise to $100 billion in 2027 next year, if economic and business conditions are favorable. It secured a $30 billion loan in September to fund its outlay.

ByteDance's spending marks a new, much more aggressive push to cement an early lead in key segments like chatbots and video, and expand its influence overseas. The Photos app works well for batch workflows. Import a set of images, review quickly, apply consistent adjustments, and export clean files. sources.title: Microsoft’s new Photos app combines your PC, OneDrive, and iCloud galleries
passages: Microsoft has redesigned its Photos app for Windows 11, overhauling the editor and image viewer, and combining photos and videos from your PC, OneDrive, and iCloud into a single space.

You can browse files online or offline, and Microsoft says photos will be available on your device “even when you’re not connected.” The new Photos editor has been “rebuilt from the ground up,” according to Microsoft, launching 25 percent faster and arranging tools into four categories: Crop, Enhance, Repair, and Stylize.
The new combined gallery experience aims to make it easier to manage and view your photos without jumping between apps or devices, while also improving app launch and scrolling performance in Photos.

extraction.body: If you’re a Windows user, you have a set of built‑in photo and video editing apps that are ready to use when you are. Microsoft Photos, Clipchamp, Paint, and Snipping Tool cover the most common editing tasks, such as cleaning up photos, cutting videos, capturing screens, and sharing results. Each app is designed for specific tasks. Together, these tools form a practical editing stack that fits into creative workflows. Each app has a clear role and, when used together, supports most everyday photo, video, and visual content tasks on Windows 11. Start here: Best built‑in Windows 11 photo editor: The Photos app The Photos app is the primary photo editor on Windows 11 and serves as a central photo library. The Photos app brings together images and videos from your PC, OneDrive, 1 and iCloud Photos, making it easy to review, organize, and share content across devices. AI‑powered tools help speed up common photo adjustments. Relight helps users change the lighting in a photo, making it easier to fine‑tune portraits or draw focus to a subject. Super resolution helps users upscale older or low‑quality photos, which can be especially useful for improving images captured on earlier mobile devices. The Photos app works well for batch workflows. Import a set of images, review quickly, apply consistent adjustments, and export clean files. Edits are non‑destructive, so you can revisit decisions without starting over. Learning keyboard and mouse shortcuts can make the Photos app feel significantly faster, especially when working through larger sets. The Photos app is designed for fast, practical edits. For complex compositing or advanced color grading, specialized tools may be a better fit. For everyday photo work, use the Photos app to keep your workflow moving. Best built‑in Windows 11 video editor: Microsoft Clipchamp Microsoft Clipchamp 2 is the built‑in AI-powered video editor available in Windows 11. Designed for modern creation workflows, Clipchamp supports both templates 3 and a full timeline, making it easy to start quickly and refine videos as needed. Trim and split clips, add captions and transitions, adjust audio, and resize your video for different platforms. Use features like automatic captions, noise suppression, and silence removal to clean things up in the background, so voice‑driven and short‑form videos take less effort to finish. When you’re ready to export, choose the highest practical resolution for where you plan to publish it. Keep your frame rate consistent, listen once more for audio balance, and give the file a clear name before saving. Best built-in app for graphics and illustration: Paint Paint has grown from a basic drawing app into a lightweight creative tool for Windows. It’s still easy to use but now offers more modern features for people who want to sketch ideas, create graphics, build layered compositions, or make AI-assisted edits. The AI tools in Paint are designed to enhance your workflow and are ideal for removing distractions or unwanted objects. For example, generative erase is one of several AI‑assisted creative tools in Paint, helping users remove unwanted elements while supporting broader composition and illustration workflows. Paint and Photos serve different but complementary creative purposes on Windows. Use Paint when you want to create, compose, or illustrate—such as building digital artwork, combining images, or restyling photos with creative effects. Use Photos when you want to enhance, touch up, organize, and export individual photos. Rather than following a linear workflow, these apps work best when you choose the one that matches your creative goal. Best for capturing and annotating content: Snipping Tool Snipping Tool has been part of Windows for years, and in Windows 11 it’s more powerful than ever, with a cleaner design, smarter shortcuts, built‑in screen recording, and productivity‑focused capture features. Snipping Tool is a fast way to capture content for tutorials, bug reports, product shots, or social posts. In addition to freeform, window, and full‑screen captures, it includes inline Quick Markup tools, a built‑in Color Picker for identifying on‑screen colors, and Perfect Screenshot—an AI‑powered capture mode that helps users get the shot they want without extra cropping. passages: Anyone who put $1,000 each into Bitcoin (CRYPTO: BTC), Ethereum (CRYPTO: ETH), XRP (CRYPTO: XRP), and Solana (CRYPTO: SOL) at the end of October 2021 has witnessed a striking difference in how $1,000 invested in crypto has fared by October 15, 2026.
Of these four investments, two have gained value while the other two have lost significant value.
Five years is just one timeframe, and different starting points can yield different results.
Even Bitcoin and XRP haven't returned to their all-time highs, with Bitcoin still far from its $126,080 peak.
This shows that which coin you choose matters more than simply investing in cryptocurrency.
Ethereum and Solana were the two most hyped coins in 2021, yet both lost money, proving excitement and network activity don't guarantee better returns.
Both of the coins that lost money had strong appeal entering late 2021.
Ethereum was seen as the backbone of the decentralized finance (DeFi) movement and the booming NFT market (digital collectibles on the blockchain).
Solana emerged as a promising alternative, boasting high speeds and low transaction fees, attracting many buyers who believed both would outperform more established cryptocurrencies.
In contrast, Ethereum dropped sharply from $4,298 to $2,426, a 44% loss that reduced the initial $1,000 investment to $564.
For investors, spreading funds across different coins may help mitigate the risks of any single investment.

Future moves could change these standings: a monthly close above $4,298 for Ethereum or $202 for Solana could erase those losses, while a monthly close below about $1.11 for XRP would erase its gains and completely alter the current balance.
XRP followed with a modest increase, rising from $1.11 to $1.33, a 19% gain that left the $1,000 stake worth $1,193.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
So, which two coins lost money, and what should investors take away from this?
Bitcoin's messaging remained consistent as a digital store of value, while XRP faced scrutiny over the SEC's lawsuit against Ripple, the company linked to the token.
The value of a cryptocurrency ultimately depends on the price paid at the beginning just as much as on the network's developments over time.

sources.title: AI Price Prediction: We Asked Grok AI Which Recovers First From the October Selloff: Bitcoin, Ethereum, XRP or Solana - AOL.com
passages: In mid-October 2026, Bitcoin (CRYPTO: BTC), Ethereum (CRYPTO: ETH), XRP (CRYPTO: XRP), and Solana (CRYPTO: SOL) all fell sharply, leaving investors wondering which cryptocurrency will recover first.
A wave of forced selling liquidated nearly $1 billion in leveraged positions.
Liquidation occurs when an exchange automatically closes a trade funded by borrowed money because the price has moved too far against it.
Grok, the AI model developed by xAI, ranks Bitcoin as the most likely to reclaim its October 13 price first, followed by Solana and XRP, with Ethereum expected to lag.
So, what factors led Grok to this conclusion, and what does it foresee for these cryptocurrencies by year-end?
Grok's conclusion is clear: Bitcoin is expected to recover first because of its shorter climb, deeper liquidity, and a robust foundation supported by institutions.
If you were to allocate a hypothetical $4,000 among these cryptocurrencies, Grok suggests putting $2,000 into Bitcoin, $800 into Solana, $700 into XRP, and $500 into Ethereum.
However, this allocation is based on Grok's analysis and should not be taken as financial advice from 24/7 Wall St.
Grok's year-end price estimates align with its recovery predictions.
The closing prices from October 13 were as follows: Bitcoin at $83,102, Ethereum at $2,496, XRP at $1.37, and Solana at $107.
Based on the October 15 prices, Bitcoin needs to gain 2.5% to return to its previous close; XRP requires a 4.2% increase, Solana a 4.3% rise, and Ethereum a 5.5% jump.
As of October 15, Bitcoin is trading at $81,052, down 2.8% over the past 24 hours.
Over the previous week, Bitcoin fluctuated between a high of $84,262 on October 12 and a low of $80,927 on October 13.
Grok cites Solana's imminent upgrade as a unique short-term catalyst.
XRP is anticipated to recover by mid-November, bolstered by a modest inflow of $740,414 on October 14, making it the only major cryptocurrency to experience inflows that day.
However, Grok notes that XRP's lower liquidity and lack of scheduled events weigh against its ranking.
Still, Bitcoin has the smallest climb ahead, while Ethereum faces the biggest challenge.
Interestingly, Grok believes Solana also has the most downside risk, potentially dropping another 15% to around $88.
Additionally, Grok argues that volatile cryptocurrencies often keep falling longer when selloffs and economic uncertainty pressure them.
Grok predicts that Bitcoin will bounce back first, potentially by October 25.
This is attributed to Bitcoin's greater liquidity, which allows large transactions without severely impacting price, and its historical appeal to institutional investors.
Solana's anticipated upgrade is scheduled for October 21 and aims to improve transaction finality to about 150 milliseconds—the time it takes for a transaction to become permanent.
If all goes well, Grok expects this upgrade could help Solana recover by about 12% over the following month, pushing prices toward the mid-$110s.
Grok highlights the trend of funds moving out of Ethereum and notes that its largest corporate investor is nearing a threshold at which buying may stop.
Solana faces the sharpest two-sided trade: a potential 15% drop to $88 if its October 21 upgrade fails, or a 12% rebound toward $115 if it succeeds.

Five years is just one timeframe, and different starting points can yield different results.

This shows that which coin you choose matters more than simply investing in cryptocurrency.

Both of the coins that lost money had strong appeal entering late 2021.
Ethereum was seen as the backbone of the decentralized finance (DeFi) movement and the booming NFT market (digital collectibles on the blockchain).
Solana emerged as a promising alternative, boasting high speeds and low transaction fees, attracting many buyers who believed both would outperform more established cryptocurrencies.
In contrast, Ethereum dropped sharply from $4,298 to $2,426, a 44% loss that reduced the initial $1,000 investment to $564.
For investors, spreading funds across different coins may help mitigate the risks of any single investment.

Anyone who put $1,000 each into Bitcoin ( CRYPTO: BTC ), Ethereum ( CRYPTO: ETH ), XRP ( CRYPTO: XRP ), and Solana ( CRYPTO: SOL ) at the end of October 2021 has witnessed a striking difference in how $1,000 invested in crypto has fared by October 15, 2026. Of these four investments, two have gained value while the other two have lost significant value.
So, which two coins lost money, and what should investors take away from this?

Bitcoin performed best, climbing from $61,340 at the end of October 2021 to $81,620 by October 15, a 33% gain that turned the $1,000 investment into $1,331. XRP followed with a modest increase, rising from $1.11 to $1.33, a 19% gain that left the $1,000 stake worth $1,193.

In contrast, Ethereum dropped sharply from $4,298 to $2,426, a 44% loss that reduced the initial $1,000 investment to $564. Solana suffered the most, falling from $202 to $104, a 48% decline that means a $1,000 investment is now worth only $515.
These results are based on hypothetical calculations using monthly closing prices, and they do not account for trading fees, spreads, or taxes, which could further affect the final numbers.

Both of the coins that lost money had strong appeal entering late 2021. Ethereum was seen as the backbone of the decentralized finance (DeFi) movement and the booming NFT market (digital collectibles on the blockchain). Solana emerged as a promising alternative, boasting high speeds and low transaction fees, attracting many buyers who believed both would outperform more established cryptocurrencies.

In contrast, Bitcoin and XRP had less hype. Bitcoin’s messaging remained consistent as a digital store of value, while XRP faced scrutiny over the SEC’s lawsuit against Ripple , the company linked to the token.

Interestingly, the two quieter coins—Bitcoin and XRP—are the only ones currently in profit. This shows that a busy network does not always lead to better returns. The value of a cryptocurrency ultimately depends on the price paid at the beginning just as much as on the network’s developments over time.
In October 2021, investors were optimistic about what Ethereum and Solana could achieve, but Ethereum has continued to lose ground to Bitcoin since then.

Five years is just one timeframe, and different starting points can yield different results. Both Ethereum and Solana remain below their October 2021 prices, highlighting that investment timing plays a significant role in performance. Even Bitcoin and XRP have n’t returned to their all-time highs, with Bitcoin still far from its $126,080 peak .

Not in this case. The two investments that initially sparked the most excitement—Ethereum and Solana—lost money, while the quieter Bitcoin and XRP thrived. This shows that which coin you choose matters more than simply investing in cryptocurrency.

For investors, spreading funds across different coins may help mitigate the risks of any single investment. Future moves could change these standings: a monthly close above $4,298 for Ethereum or $202 for Solana could erase those losses, while a monthly close below about $1.11 for XRP would erase its gains and completely alter the current balance.

passages: In mid-October 2026, Bitcoin (CRYPTO: BTC), Ethereum (CRYPTO: ETH), XRP (CRYPTO: XRP), and Solana (CRYPTO: SOL) all fell sharply, leaving investors wondering which cryptocurrency will recover first.
A wave of forced selling liquidated nearly $1 billion in leveraged positions.
Liquidation occurs when an exchange automatically closes a trade funded by borrowed money because the price has moved too far against it.
Grok, the AI model developed by xAI, ranks Bitcoin as the most likely to reclaim its October 13 price first, followed by Solana and XRP, with Ethereum expected to lag.
So, what factors led Grok to this conclusion, and what does it foresee for these cryptocurrencies by year-end?
Grok's conclusion is clear: Bitcoin is expected to recover first because of its shorter climb, deeper liquidity, and a robust foundation supported by institutions.
If you were to allocate a hypothetical $4,000 among these cryptocurrencies, Grok suggests putting $2,000 into Bitcoin, $800 into Solana, $700 into XRP, and $500 into Ethereum.
However, this allocation is based on Grok's analysis and should not be taken as financial advice from 24/7 Wall St.
Grok's year-end price estimates align with its recovery predictions.
The closing prices from October 13 were as follows: Bitcoin at $83,102, Ethereum at $2,496, XRP at $1.37, and Solana at $107.
Based on the October 15 prices, Bitcoin needs to gain 2.5% to return to its previous close; XRP requires a 4.2% increase, Solana a 4.3% rise, and Ethereum a 5.5% jump.
As of October 15, Bitcoin is trading at $81,052, down 2.8% over the past 24 hours.
Over the previous week, Bitcoin fluctuated between a high of $84,262 on October 12 and a low of $80,927 on October 13.
Grok cites Solana's imminent upgrade as a unique short-term catalyst.
XRP is anticipated to recover by mid-November, bolstered by a modest inflow of $740,414 on October 14, making it the only major cryptocurrency to experience inflows that day.

This is attributed to Bitcoin's greater liquidity, which allows large transactions without severely impacting price, and its historical appeal to institutional investors.
Solana's anticipated upgrade is scheduled for October 21 and aims to improve transaction finality to about 150 milliseconds—the time it takes for a transaction to become permanent.

Grok highlights the trend of funds moving out of Ethereum and notes that its largest corporate investor is nearing a threshold at which buying may stop.
Solana faces the sharpest two-sided trade: a potential 15% drop to $88 if its October 21 upgrade fails, or a 12% rebound toward $115 if it succeeds.

Investors withdrew a significant $391 million from Bitcoin ( CRYPTO:BTC ) and Ethereum ( CRYPTO:ETH ) exchange-traded funds (ETFs), according to SoSoValue. Bitcoin ETFs lost $261.46 million, while Ethereum ETFs saw outflows of $129.51 million. In contrast, XRP ( CRYPTO:XRP ) funds experienced a positive shift, with XRP ETF inflows reaching $740,414, making it the only fund group among the four major cryptocurrencies to see any inflow. This marks a reversal from the previous day, when Bitcoin ETFs recorded their second-largest inflow of the month on October 13, while XRP funds saw zero activity. This fueled speculation that funds were shifting from XRP to Bitcoin. What does this one-day opposite pattern indicate? Bitcoin’s $261.46 million outflow was the second-highest of October , following the October 7 session. It completely negated the $175.62 million that had come into Bitcoin funds on October 13. Nevertheless, Bitcoin funds still hold a substantial $104.83 billion in net assets. Ethereum funds also faced a setback, shedding $129.51 million the same day, adding to selling pressure on the two largest cryptocurrencies. Meanwhile, Solana ( CRYPTO:SOL ) funds fell slightly, shedding $1.29 million. Although small, this marks the ninth out of ten October sessions in which Solana funds have faced outflows, highlighting an ongoing trend. Meanwhile, XRP funds recorded an inflow for the first time after three consecutive sessions with no activity. A fund records a flow when large brokers create new fund shares by depositing cash, or redeem shares for cash. For three sessions, these brokers were inactive, making the $740,414 inflow a notable shift, as it indicates a change from inactivity to some movement. Despite the positive inflow, the amount that entered XRP funds is a mere fraction of what left Bitcoin funds that same day—less than 0.3%. Therefore, treating these two events as comparable would not be accurate. Each fund’s figures must be viewed independently. While Bitcoin funds are experiencing outflows, XRP funds have recorded inflows, yet there’s no evidence suggesting that investors are necessarily switching from Bitcoin to XRP. One creation of new XRP fund shares does not guarantee that these buyers will return for subsequent sessions. To date, XRP funds have attracted $1.80 billion since launch, reflecting net cash invested by investors. However, their current net assets stand at $1.51 billion, approximately 16.3% less than the total invested amount. This means XRP fund holders are currently at an average loss. On October 13, Bitcoin funds saw positive inflows while XRP funds remained stagnant, suggesting a rotation of investor funds. The following day, however, the trend flipped, with Bitcoin funds losing money while XRP funds posted the only inflow. This shift raises questions about investor sentiment, but both interpretations can’t be correct at the same time. This contradiction emphasizes the unpredictability of daily flows . A single day’s data may reflect actions from a single large investor reallocating assets or trivial market noise. A more reliable indicator would require observing the same trend across consecutive days. Solana’s nine negative sessions out of ten in October illustrate this point, while XRP’s single positive session does not provide similar confidence. The recent inflow could signal renewed interest or be an isolated event that may not repeat. A single inflow of $740,414 does not provide enough evidence to conclude that demand is steadily increasing. Currently, XRP fund demand appears largely unchanged compared to the period before October 14, but the inactivity has changed; there’s no longer a flat line. A minor inflow following three sessions of inactivity does not constitute a trend. Bitcoin funds show the same volatility, swinging from a $175.62 million inflow to a $261.46 million outflow in back-to-back sessions. For XRP funds to show sustained demand, they would need inflows over at least three consecutive sessions, matching the three-session inactivity period they recently ended. Furthermore, if net assets were to increase by about 19.5%, approaching the $1.80 billion cumulative inflow, holders could potentially break even. Until both conditions are met, the October 14 inflow should be viewed as a market pulse, with subsequent data from SoSoValue likely confirming or reversing this reading. It completely negated the $175.62 million that had come into Bitcoin funds on October 13.
Nevertheless, Bitcoin funds still hold a substantial $104.83 billion in net assets.
Currently, XRP fund demand appears largely unchanged compared to the period before October 14, but the inactivity has changed; there’s no longer a flat line.
A minor inflow following three sessions of inactivity does not constitute a trend.
Ethereum ETFs pulled in $690 million one week, then sent investors rushing for the exits the next.
This shift raises questions about investor sentiment, but both interpretations can’t be correct at the same time.
Despite the positive inflow, the amount that entered XRP funds is a mere fraction of what left Bitcoin funds that same day—less than 0.3%.

Each fund’s figures must be viewed independently.
One creation of new XRP fund shares does not guarantee that these buyers will return for subsequent sessions.
Bitcoin ETFs are pulling in hundreds of millions while XRP funds sit frozen with zero net flow for three straight sessions, and the source of that capital tells a story investors may not expect.

U.S. investors pulled money from Solana ETFs for seven of eight straight trading sessions in October, yet a Hong Kong asset manager chose that exact moment to launch a brand-new spot Solana fund.
The answer reveals a hidden pattern that repeats every three months across crypto markets.

Investors withdrew a significant $391 million from Bitcoin ( CRYPTO:BTC ) and Ethereum ( CRYPTO:ETH ) exchange-traded funds (ETFs), according to SoSoValue. Bitcoin ETFs lost $261.46 million, while Ethereum ETFs saw outflows of $129.51 million. In contrast, XRP ( CRYPTO:XRP ) funds experienced a positive shift, with XRP ETF inflows reaching $740,414, making it the only fund group among the four major cryptocurrencies to see any inflow. This marks a reversal from the previous day, when Bitcoin ETFs recorded their second-largest inflow of the month on October 13, while XRP funds saw zero activity. This fueled speculation that funds were shifting from XRP to Bitcoin. What does this one-day opposite pattern indicate? Bitcoin’s $261.46 million outflow was the second-highest of October , following the October 7 session. It completely negated the $175.62 million that had come into Bitcoin funds on October 13. Nevertheless, Bitcoin funds still hold a substantial $104.83 billion in net assets. Ethereum funds also faced a setback, shedding $129.51 million the same day, adding to selling pressure on the two largest cryptocurrencies. Meanwhile, Solana ( CRYPTO:SOL ) funds fell slightly, shedding $1.29 million. Although small, this marks the ninth out of ten October sessions in which Solana funds have faced outflows, highlighting an ongoing trend. Meanwhile, XRP funds recorded an inflow for the first time after three consecutive sessions with no activity. A fund records a flow when large brokers create new fund shares by depositing cash, or redeem shares for cash. For three sessions, these brokers were inactive, making the $740,414 inflow a notable shift, as it indicates a change from inactivity to some movement. Despite the positive inflow, the amount that entered XRP funds is a mere fraction of what left Bitcoin funds that same day—less than 0.3%. Therefore, treating these two events as comparable would not be accurate. Each fund’s figures must be viewed independently. While Bitcoin funds are experiencing outflows, XRP funds have recorded inflows, yet there’s no evidence suggesting that investors are necessarily switching from Bitcoin to XRP. One creation of new XRP fund shares does not guarantee that these buyers will return for subsequent sessions. To date, XRP funds have attracted $1.80 billion since launch, reflecting net cash invested by investors. However, their current net assets stand at $1.51 billion, approximately 16.3% less than the total invested amount. This means XRP fund holders are currently at an average loss. On October 13, Bitcoin funds saw positive inflows while XRP funds remained stagnant, suggesting a rotation of investor funds. The following day, however, the trend flipped, with Bitcoin funds losing money while XRP funds posted the only inflow. This shift raises questions about investor sentiment, but both interpretations can’t be correct at the same time. This contradiction emphasizes the unpredictability of daily flows . A single day’s data may reflect actions from a single large investor reallocating assets or trivial market noise. A more reliable indicator would require observing the same trend across consecutive days. Solana’s nine negative sessions out of ten in October illustrate this point, while XRP’s single positive session does not provide similar confidence. The recent inflow could signal renewed interest or be an isolated event that may not repeat. A single inflow of $740,414 does not provide enough evidence to conclude that demand is steadily increasing. Currently, XRP fund demand appears largely unchanged compared to the period before October 14, but the inactivity has changed; there’s no longer a flat line. A minor inflow following three sessions of inactivity does not constitute a trend. Bitcoin funds show the same volatility, swinging from a $175.62 million inflow to a $261.46 million outflow in back-to-back sessions. For XRP funds to show sustained demand, they would need inflows over at least three consecutive sessions, matching the three-session inactivity period they recently ended. Furthermore, if net assets were to increase by about 19.5%, approaching the $1.80 billion cumulative inflow, holders could potentially break even. Until both conditions are met, the October 14 inflow should be viewed as a market pulse, with subsequent data from SoSoValue likely confirming or reversing this reading. story.title: If You Put $1,000 Each Into Bitcoin, Ethereum, XRP and Solana Five Years Ago, Two Would Have Lost Money. - 24/7 Wall St.

facts.text: Anyone who put $1,000 each into Bitcoin (CRYPTO: BTC), Ethereum (CRYPTO: ETH), XRP (CRYPTO: XRP), and Solana (CRYPTO: SOL) at the end of October 2021 has witnessed a striking difference in how $1,000 invested in crypto has fared by October 15, 2026.
Of these four investments, two have gained value while the other two have lost significant value.
Five years is just one timeframe, and different starting points can yield different results.
Even Bitcoin and XRP haven't returned to their all-time highs, with Bitcoin still far from its $126,080 peak.
This shows that which coin you choose matters more than simply investing in cryptocurrency.
Ethereum and Solana were the two most hyped coins in 2021, yet both lost money, proving excitement and network activity don't guarantee better returns.
In contrast, Ethereum dropped sharply from $4,298 to $2,426, a 44% loss that reduced the initial $1,000 investment to $564.
Both of the coins that lost money had strong appeal entering late 2021.
Ethereum was seen as the backbone of the decentralized finance (DeFi) movement and the booming NFT market (digital collectibles on the blockchain).
Solana emerged as a promising alternative, boasting high speeds and low transaction fees, attracting many buyers who believed both would outperform more established cryptocurrencies.
For investors, spreading funds across different coins may help mitigate the risks of any single investment.

Future moves could change these standings: a monthly close above $4,298 for Ethereum or $202 for Solana could erase those losses, while a monthly close below about $1.11 for XRP would erase its gains and completely alter the current balance.
XRP followed with a modest increase, rising from $1.11 to $1.33, a 19% gain that left the $1,000 stake worth $1,193.
So, which two coins lost money, and what should investors take away from this?
Bitcoin's messaging remained consistent as a digital store of value, while XRP faced scrutiny over the SEC's lawsuit against Ripple, the company linked to the token.
The value of a cryptocurrency ultimately depends on the price paid at the beginning just as much as on the network's developments over time.

passages: Massive Expansion of AI Compute Capacity AWS offers the widest range of GPU-based instances of any cloud provider to power a diverse set of AI and machine learning workloads.
At NVIDIA GTC 2026, AWS announced plans to add more than 1 million NVIDIA GPUs starting in 2026.
Since then, demand has exceeded those expectations.
This additional capacity will help power customer workloads ranging from agentic AI and scientific discovery to enterprise automation and physical AI.
In addition, AWS will expand NVIDIA Blackwell capacity, including NVIDIA RTX PRO™ 4500 Blackwell Server Edition GPUs for Amazon EC2 G7 instances .
G7 instances deliver 4.6x AI inference performance and 2.1x graphics performance compared to previous-generation G6 instances.
AWS and NVIDIA are also collaborating on NVIDIA Spectrum™ networking to further optimize network performance for large-scale AI training workloads across GPU clusters.

26, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Amazon Web Services (AWS), an Amazon.com, Inc. company (NASDAQ: AMZN), and NVIDIA (NASDAQ: NVDA) today announced a major expansion of their strategic collaboration to meet surging global demand for AI infrastructure as demand continues to accelerate.

Building on already-rapid customer adoption of NVIDIA-accelerated compute on AWS, the companies plan to deploy 2 million additional NVIDIA GPUs across AWS’s global infrastructure and deepen their work together across AI factories, CPUs, networking, open models, data processing and robotics, delivering co-engineered AI solutions that enable customers to accelerate AI development and deployment at unprecedented scale.
“NVIDIA and AWS have built one of the great growth engines of the AI era, and demand is running ahead of every forecast,” said Jensen Huang, founder and CEO of NVIDIA.
“For 16 years, we have scaled NVIDIA computing in the cloud together.
This expansion reflects customers’ demand for NVIDIA’s platform on AWS.”
Copies of reports filed with the SEC are posted on the company’s website and are available from NVIDIA without charge.

These forward-looking statements are not guarantees of future performance and speak only as of the date hereof, and, except as required by law, NVIDIA disclaims any obligation to update these forward-looking statements to reflect future events or circumstances.
Purpose-built for the next generation of AI, Vera complements AWS’s strategy to offer the broadest choice of compute — from AWS custom silicon to the latest accelerators and CPUs from partners.
Powering Federal AI at the Highest Levels of Security Government agencies need secure AI infrastructure to keep pace with the demands of national security.

Heterogeneous AI Infrastructure Using NVIDIA NVLink Fusion With NVHBM At re:Invent 2025, AWS announced support for NVIDIA NVLink Fusion high-speed chip interconnect technology in next-generation Trainium chips.

NVIDIA and Amazon’s Annapurna Labs are expanding that support to work on NVIDIA’s new custom high-bandwidth memory (NVHBM) technology , in partnership with memory suppliers, which would give Trainium access to faster, more power-efficient memory.

Combined with NVLink Fusion, Annapurna Labs can now tap NVIDIA’s custom memory technology and scale-up architecture to enhance performance and efficiency for AI workloads while seamlessly integrating Trainium and GPUs within a common rack-scale architecture.
As part of the expanded collaboration, the companies are working to:
“Customers want the freedom to choose the best tools for their AI workloads, and they want confidence that everything works seamlessly together,” said Matt Garman, CEO of AWS.
“That’s why we’ve invested deeply with NVIDIA to make AWS the best place to run NVIDIA AI technologies, optimizing performance across our infrastructure from networking and security to deployment.
This expanded collaboration gives frontier labs, enterprises and governments even more ways to build and deploy AI on AWS.”

BOLD, led by the University of Oxford, is developing approaches that help AI systems learn, adapt and operate alongside people. extraction.body: NVIDIA today announced a five-year compute donation valued at $250 million to strengthen the United Kingdom’s agentic safety and security research capability. The commitment will provide $50 million in compute access annually to support agentic safety and security research across the U.K. The majority will support the wider U.K. AI safety and security research community, with a proportion supporting work with the British Open-Ended Learning and Discovery Lab (BOLD), the Science of Fundamental AI Research Lab (SOFAIR) and Imperial College London. “AI capability and safety must advance together,” said Jensen Huang, founder and CEO of NVIDIA. “The U.K. brings world-class scientific rigor to this essential engineering challenge. With this $250 million commitment, NVIDIA will put accelerated computing in the hands of U.K. researchers to develop, test and strengthen safeguards for increasingly powerful AI. This is how the U.K. turns research leadership into real-world solutions — and scientific progress into a future that benefits everyone.” “This commitment is a vote of confidence in our world-leading strength and expertise in AI research — and, in particular, frontier AI safety that is becoming ever more important as AI’s capabilities develop,” said U.K. AI Minister Kanishka Narayan. “NVIDIA’s donation will help Britain’s AI innovators access the resources they need to bring their ideas to life — and, in the process, help build a distinctly British AI future that is safe, secure and that serves people’s best interests, objectives that will be central to the U.K.’s G20 presidency.” “To realise the opportunities of AI, people need to feel the technology is safe and secure. The government is committed to ensuring AI can be securely harnessed to fuel new discoveries and drive growth,“ said U.K. Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds. “NVIDIA’s investment will help British researchers continue to lead the world in that effort — accelerating the breakthroughs that build trust and help us deploy AI safely.” Strengthening UK Leadership in Agentic Safety and Security Compute provided through the initiative will be dedicated to agentic safety and security research. The program will connect complementary areas of U.K. research, including in AI safety and security. BOLD, led by the University of Oxford, is developing approaches that help AI systems learn, adapt and operate alongside people. SOFAIR, led by UCL, is exploring new open source AI architectures and more accessible ways to develop and deploy AI. Imperial’s work will include safety engineering and robotics. “We are experiencing a critical moment where AI safety as an afterthought is no longer appropriate for the open-ended, evolving world,” said Jakob Foerster, founding director of BOLD. “This compute will help us explore transparent and human-centric approaches to AI that allow us to collectively rise to the challenge by building in governance and human-AI co-improvement from the ground up.” “The next frontier of artificial intelligence is physical — robots, autonomous systems of agents that perceive, reason and act in the real world,” said Alessandra Russo, director of Imperial Frontier AI Research Lab and convening co-director of Human and AI, School of Convergence Science. “With NVIDIA and our industry partners, Imperial is working to ensure that safety and assurance is at the heart of this revolution, ensuring the U.K. leads not only in developing physical AI but in making it trustworthy for the communities and industries that will depend on it.” NVIDIA will fund compute access through U.K.-based NVIDIA Cloud Partners , with infrastructure hosted in the U.K. This will support the U.K. compute ecosystem and provide a domestic platform for research. Provider selection, technical architecture and commercial terms are to be agreed. As part of the wider initiative, research programs will focus on secure agents, open-model security and real-world threat mitigations. The work will support secure sandboxes, reproducible research and safety assessment benchmarks, including research conducted using NVIDIA OpenShell™ open, secure runtime software and the NVIDIA Sentry reference design . Findings are intended to inform safeguards across the wider computing ecosystem. The commitment builds on NVIDIA’s collaboration with the U.K.’s research community, including on the University of Bristol’s Isambard-AI supercomputer, powered by NVIDIA Grace Hopper Superchips. passages: In June 2026, the Financial Stability Board (FSB) published its consultation report, “ Sound Practices for Responsible Adoption of Artificial Intelligence (AI) .” Rather than creating new international standards, the report distills governance practices already emerging across leading financial institutions into twelve nonbinding recommended practices covering the full AI life cycle.

This memorandum is provided by Skadden, Arps, Slate, Meagher & Flom LLP and its affiliates for educational and informational purposes only and is not intended and should not be construed as legal advice.

Meanwhile, although the recommended practices remain nonbinding, the consultation underscores the FSB’s continued focus on promoting consistent approaches to AI governance across the global financial sector.
The report is significant because it consolidates supervisory thinking into a coherent governance framework.

For multinational financial institutions, the FSB framework provides a practical operating model that can be used as a common global baseline while accommodating jurisdiction-specific legal requirements.
The 12 sound practices are best understood as concrete governance actions to guide sound enterprise-wide implementation.

Drawing on case studies from banks and insurers, it illustrates (i) how institutions are deploying AI in production, (ii) the governance challenges they have encountered and (iii) the controls they have implemented.

extraction.body: In June 2026, the Financial Stability Board (FSB) published its consultation report, “ Sound Practices for Responsible Adoption of Artificial Intelligence (AI) .” Rather than creating new international standards, the report distills governance practices already emerging across leading financial institutions into twelve nonbinding recommended practices covering the full AI life cycle. The report is notable for its practical focus. Drawing on case studies from banks and insurers, it illustrates (i) how institutions are deploying AI in production, (ii) the governance challenges they have encountered and (iii) the controls they have implemented. Rather than prescribing particular technologies, the report focuses on governance, accountability, documentation and life-cycle risk management. extraction.body: Lawyers for the Profession® Alert | 5 min read The Florida Bar has concluded that a lawyer may utilize generative artificial intelligence (AI) so long as the lawyer can reasonably guarantee compliance with the lawyer's ethical obligations. The release of ChatGPT-3 in November 2022 prompted a wide-ranging discussion on lawyer use of generative AI in the practice of law. Generative AI is a "deep-learning model" that compiles data to generate statistically probable outputs when prompted and is capable of analyzing documents and drafting entire briefs. While it has the potential to improve a lawyer's efficiency, generative AI is still in its infancy and prone to "hallucinate" or create answers that sound convincing. The Florida Bar cited a recent case in the Southern District of New York where a federal judge sanctioned two lawyers and their law firm following their use of false citations created by generative AI. [1] Citing the Rules Regulating the Florida Bar, which govern a lawyer's ethical duties and are adopted from the ABA Model Rules, [2] the advisory opinion addressed four specific ethical pitfalls when using generative AI: A lawyer's ethical duties under Rule 1.6 are broad and far-reaching. Absent the client's informed consent or some applicable exception, a lawyer may not reveal confidential information. This advisory opinion recommends that a lawyer obtain the affected client's informed consent prior to utilizing a third-party generative AI tool if the utilization would involve the disclosure of confidential information. Another consideration under Rule 1.6 when using generative AI is a lawyer's duty to prevent the inadvertent or unauthorized disclosure of confidential information. Because generative AI is self-learning, it may, as it continues to add inputs to existing parameters, reveal a client's information in response to future prompts by third parties. The opinion recommended the following to protect client information: Confidentiality concerns may be mitigated by the use of an in-house AI program where it does not disclose confidential information to a third party, thus removing the obligation on the lawyer to obtain informed consent. The advisory opinion addressed generative AI use by a nonlawyer and applied the standards under Rule 5.3 (Responsibilities Regarding Nonlawyer Assistance): A lawyer should also consider what tasks it may ethically delegate to generative AI. For example, a lawyer cannot delegate to AI functions that require a lawyer's personal judgment and participation such that they would constitute the practice of law. If a lawyer is using AI to conduct interviews with prospective clients, the obligations set forth in Rule 1.18 (Duties to Prospective Client) would apply. Those parameters would mean that the AI program must: Rule 1.5 prohibits attorneys from collecting an unreasonable fee. The increased efficiency from the proper use of generative AI must not result in duplicate charges or falsely inflated billable hours. Based on existing standards, the Florida Bar reached the opinion that lawyers should inform a client, preferably in writing, of the lawyer's intent to charge the client the actual cost of using generative AI. If the actual cost associated with a client's matter cannot be determined, a lawyer should not prorate the periodic charges of generative AI (if any) but should instead account for those charges as overhead. Finally, the opinion concluded that while a lawyer may charge a client for reasonable time spent on case-specific research, a lawyer should be careful not to charge for time spent developing minimal competence in the use of generative AI. A lawyer should be careful when using generative AI chatbots for advertising and intake purposes, as the lawyer will be ultimately responsible should the chatbot provide misleading information to prospective clients or communicate in a manner that is inappropriately intrusive or coercive. To safeguard against such risks, a lawyer must inform prospective clients that they are communicating with an AI program. Additionally, a lawyer using an AI chatbot should consider including screening questions that limit the chatbot's communications if another lawyer already represents that person. A lawyer may ethically utilize generative AI technologies, but only to the extent that a lawyer can reasonably guarantee compliance with all existing ethical obligations. Another consideration under Rule 1.6 when using generative AI is a lawyer's duty to prevent the inadvertent or unauthorized disclosure of confidential information. Because generative AI is self-learning, it may, as it continues to add inputs to existing parameters, reveal a client's information in response to future prompts by third parties. The opinion recommended the following to protect client information:

Confidentiality concerns may be mitigated by the use of an in-house AI program where it does not disclose confidential information to a third party, thus removing the obligation on the lawyer to obtain informed consent.

If a lawyer is using AI to conduct interviews with prospective clients, the obligations set forth in Rule 1.18 (Duties to Prospective Client) would apply.
Those parameters would mean that the AI program must:

Rule 1.5 prohibits attorneys from collecting an unreasonable fee. The increased efficiency from the proper use of generative AI must not result in duplicate charges or falsely inflated billable hours. Based on existing standards, the Florida Bar reached the opinion that lawyers should inform a client, preferably in writing, of the lawyer's intent to charge the client the actual cost of using generative AI.

If the actual cost associated with a client's matter cannot be determined, a lawyer should not prorate the periodic charges of generative AI (if any) but should instead account for those charges as overhead. Finally, the opinion concluded that while a lawyer may charge a client for reasonable time spent on case-specific research, a lawyer should be careful not to charge for time spent developing minimal competence in the use of generative AI.

A lawyer should be careful when using generative AI chatbots for advertising and intake purposes, as the lawyer will be ultimately responsible should the chatbot provide misleading information to prospective clients or communicate in a manner that is inappropriately intrusive or coercive.

extraction.body: A Texas company has plans to use a site at the Natural Energy Laboratory of Hawaii Authority’s Hawaii Ocean Science and Technology Park in Kailua-Kona to make jet fuel from seawater. A Texas company has plans to use a site at the Natural Energy Laboratory of Hawaii Authority’s Hawaii Ocean Science and Technology Park in Kailua-Kona to make jet fuel from seawater. The state’s Office of Planning and Sustainable Development on Monday published a draft environmental assessment with a finding of no significant environmental impact for the project proposal by Sea Dragon Energy Inc. of Florence, Texas, a small town about 40 miles north of Austin. “Our desire is to meet the specifications for JP-5,” Tracy Kriewald, Sea Dragon Energy’s vice president of engineering, told the Tribune-Herald on Monday. Jet Propellant-5, also known as JP-5, is a type of jet fuel used in military aircraft, mostly Navy aircraft that take off and land from aircraft carriers. It’s a flammable liquid that smells like kerosene and is made from hydrocarbons, which are compounds found in crude oil. The facility, when and if built, would be a research-and-development laboratory for Sea Dragon’s Project GENESIS. According to Sea Dragon’s website, the aim of the project is to refine the efficiency of a technology patented by the Naval Research Laboratory to allow extraction of carbon dioxide from seawater and simultaneously produce hydrogen. “The ocean is an incredible reservoir with over 140 times the carbon dioxide concentration compared to air, and it also contains hydrogen, which is another important component in making SAF” — which is an acronym for “sustainable aviation fuel” — according to Sea Dragon’s website. Sea Dragon said the next-generation aviation fuel-making process will have both military and commercial applications. NELHA’s HOST Park extracts seawater from depths of up to 3,000 feet below the ocean’s surface which, according to Kriewald, is what makes the Kona site attractive to Sea Dragon. “We want to go there because they have great seawater and seawater infrastructure,” he said. “We want the nice, clean seawater to make it easier for us. “We won’t have to do a lot of pre-treatment of the water.” While the potential of the project appears to be as vast as the ocean itself, the technology is in its infancy. According to the draft EA, the process will require the monthly extraction of 449,000 gallons of seawater through NELHA’s seawater system, 50,000 gallons of fresh water, and 70 kilograms of supplemental hydrogen (H2) gas to produce 10 gallons of aviation fuel. Byproducts of the process will include hydrocarbon gases equivalent to a gallon of fuel and 80 gallons of water. According to Kriewald, the seawater and fresh water will be returned to the source — the ocean, in the case of the seawater. The fresh water might come from the Department of Water Supply, although the document indicates an alternative source is being considered. The supplemental hydrogen could come from a production facility at the HOST Park, although commercial alternatives also are available. “For every gallon of ocean water that we use, we put a gallon back in. We don’t use any water. We just extract the CO2 that’s embedded in it,” Kriewald said. The facility, which is projected to cost between $12 million and $20 million, would be built in an already existing building that formerly housed a bottler of desalinated seawater. “No new buildings, substantial land disturbances, or substantial new outdoor equipment are proposed,” the draft EA states. Project GENESIS, if successful, could lead to the development of a larger seawater-to-jet fuel industry. “This might be the first integrated end-to-end process that we know of, in which one company is responsible for everything for direct ocean capture,” Kriewald said. “But this is not a manufacturing facility, at all. That’s not our job. “This project is to learn how to improve efficiency.” According to the draft EA, Sea Dragon will be responsible for decommissioning the equipment at the facility at the completion of the R&D period. “We’re a research lab, and we’ll always be a research lab,” Kriewald said. “We’ll be there maybe four to five years to do research on different things as the technology changes. “It’s a very interesting technology, and it could be something that’s very valuable for the future.” Sea Dragon representatives, according to Kriewald, will be at the HOST Park’s 50th Anniversary Open House from 10 a.m. to 3 p.m. Saturday, Oct. 19. The draft EA, which can be found at bit.ly/4ehrY4q, triggers at 30-day public comment period.

sources.title: Sea Dragon Energy comes to Kona’s technology park to turn seawater into jet fuel - Big Island Now
passages: With the technologies developed, Sea Dragon has chosen to set up shop at Kona’s technology park to prove the concept of seawater to jet fuel works.
The company’s mission is to address a critical challenge for military operations and remote communities: the dependence on extensive, often vulnerable fuel-supply chains.

“I would wager that just about everyone here, when they first heard it, said it must be the craziest idea ever,” said John Kohut, chairman and CEO of Sea Dragon Energy. “I know I did when I first heard it.”
“I literally run on jet fuel, and a lot of Kona coffee,” Tokuda said with a laugh.
Tokuda said the Big Island and the state have had a rough year, with communities suffering damage from Kona low storms to an earthquake in South Kona to Hurricanes Lala, Lowell and Nolo.
These disasters are a reminder of the critical need to ensure the islands have access to resources.

On Wednesday, Kohut spoke to a group of community and business leaders at a traditional Hawaiian blessing the company held at its warehouse located at the Hawai‘i Ocean Science Technology Park in Kailua-Kona that is operated by the Natural Energy Laboratory of Hawaiʻi Authority.

But on a more serious note, she said: “It reminds me how important it is to have safe, responsible jet fuel being produced throughout our country, throughout our world, and especially right here on our islands.”

“Over the last four years or more, we’ve been on contract under the Office of Naval Research to develop these technologies, to integrate this together, and demonstrate the capability, and prove that this type of fuel can, in fact, be totally synthesized from seawater,” Kohut said.

What the authority tries to do, Olson said, is bring in new companies, like Sea Dragon, that would utilize either the deep or the surface-sea water or both, and then create new technologies and a business, which would then be employing people that live here on the island.
By developing technology that produces drop-in aviation fuel from seawater and power, the company seeks to reduce logistics burdens, strengthen fuel independence and enhance operational readiness.
In the next two years, the energy company hopes to refine the technology, work with catalysts and try to figure out how they can produce the fuel as efficiently as possible.

extraction.body: "I would wager that just about everyone here, when they first heard it, said it must be the craziest idea ever," said John Kohut, chairman and CEO of the energy company operating on the Big Island. "I know I did when I first heard it." It sounds like science fiction, but the leader of an energy company operating on the Big Island said this idea could soon become a reality. “I would wager that just about everyone here, when they first heard it, said it must be the craziest idea ever,” said John Kohut, chairman and CEO of Sea Dragon Energy. “I know I did when I first heard it.” On Wednesday, Kohut spoke to a group of community and business leaders at a traditional Hawaiian blessing the company held at its warehouse located at the Hawai‘i Ocean Science Technology Park in Kailua-Kona that is operated by the Natural Energy Laboratory of Hawaiʻi Authority. Suzanne Shaske, director of operations of engineering at Sea Dragon, led a tour of the facility’s emerging fuel-production technology. “Today’s milestone represents an important step in Sea Dragon’s proof-of-capability program,” Kohut said. “Producing our first fuel demonstrates the advancement of our efforts to develop distributed, modular and scalable systems capable of producing fuel at or near the point of need.” The large facility is not producing fuel yet, but the company expects it will have samples created by early 2027. The long-term goal is to create fuel on a barge at sea that would be used by the military. Kohut said seawater-to-jet fuel is based on sound science and technologies, some of which were invented more than 100 years ago, and others that are much more recent. Jet fuel is a combination of certain hydrocarbon molecules made up of hydrogen and carbon. There are seven major steps that Sea Dragon will be integrating at the facility and proving so they can ultimately scale up. “The bottom line is, first, you extract carbon dioxide from seawater and ultimately convert it into carbon monoxide,” Kohut said. “Also, from water, you can get hydrogen.” With the carbon and hydrogen, engineers at Sea Dragon will use the Fischer-Tropsch skid to produce hydrocarbons. From there, Sea Dragon will refine, distill and get the right mix of hydrocarbons and additives to meet the requirements for specific jet fuels. The technology breakthrough to convert seawater to jet fuel was developed by the U.S. Naval Research Laboratory in 2014. The Navy then awarded a $9.4 million contract to Sea Dragon Energy in August 2025 to fund the research into what it would take to develop the jet fuel on scale, according to the U.S. Department of War. “Not to be melodramatic, but today you’re witnessing that next step of a very collective and engaged and resilient partnership as we challenge our Sea Dragon teammates to move the dream of science into reality of jet fuel,” said Mat Winter, retired vice admiral from the U.S. Navy. Winter told the group he had a front-row seat to the discovery in 2014. He was working hand-in-hand with the Naval Research Laboratory scientists who were taking the seawater-to-jet-fuel science and putting it together so companies, specifically Sea Dragon, could then license, mature and produce it. “As we look at this science and, I’ll say, transition to reality, you’re going to realize that this is a pivotal change for our Navy,” Winter said. “The ability to actually provide the fuels needed at the point of need (on the sea). That’s an incredible opportunity.” While it’s still in the exploratory phase to determine if jet fuel created from water will be able to be produced on a large scale, Winter said, Sea Dragon will take that dream and move it forward. “It’s much more mature than it has been,” Winter said. With the technologies developed, Sea Dragon has chosen to set up shop at Kona’s technology park to prove the concept of seawater to jet fuel works. The company’s mission is to address a critical challenge for military operations and remote communities: the dependence on extensive, often vulnerable fuel-supply chains. By developing technology that produces drop-in aviation fuel from seawater and power, the company seeks to reduce logistics burdens, strengthen fuel independence and enhance operational readiness. “Over the last four years or more, we’ve been on contract under the Office of Naval Research to develop these technologies, to integrate this together, and demonstrate the capability, and prove that this type of fuel can, in fact, be totally synthesized from seawater,” Kohut said. In the next two years, the energy company hopes to refine the technology, work with catalysts and try to figure out how they can produce the fuel as efficiently as possible. “Because that’s the name of the game,” Kohut said. “It’s efficiency. It’s ultimately, how much does a gallon of jet fuel cost when we’re complete with the process?” Also, Kohut said the other big piece is how that fuel is being delivered. “The next step is to move from here onto a barge,” he told the group. “Our plan is to move this technology onto maritime vessels.” Keith Olson, interim executive director of the Natural Energy Laboratory of Hawaiʻi Authority, said the state agency provides deep and surface-sea water to clients at the technology park. What the authority tries to do, Olson said, is bring in new companies, like Sea Dragon, that would utilize either the deep or the surface-sea water or both, and then create new technologies and a business, which would then be employing people that live here on the island. “They fit perfectly because they’re going to be utilizing our deep-ocean water for their feed for the CO2 (carbon dioxide) that they need to create,” Olson said. Hawai‘i U.S. Rep. Jill Tokuda was among the guest speakers on Wednesday. She noted that as she flew into the Big Island, she has officially flown a million miles. “I literally run on jet fuel, and a lot of Kona coffee,” Tokuda said with a laugh. But on a more serious note, she said: “It reminds me how important it is to have safe, responsible jet fuel being produced throughout our country, throughout our world, and especially right here on our islands.” Tokuda said the Big Island and the state have had a rough year, with communities suffering damage from Kona low storms to an earthquake in South Kona to Hurricanes Lala, Lowell and Nolo. These disasters are a reminder of the critical need to ensure the islands have access to resources. “When I think about companies like Sea Dragon Energy, when I think about the groundbreaking work and research that you will do here, I can’t help but think about the greatest resource we will bring to the table and to your endeavors: our people,” Tokuda said. “The very best and the brightest you will find anywhere in the world, I would argue, totally biased, but the ones that we want to make sure can see a future for themselves right here at home in Hawaiʻi.” Tokuda said too many keiki (children) think they have to travel a million miles away to find opportunities.
