It sounds like science fiction, but the leader of an energy company operating on the Big Island said this idea could soon become a reality.

“I would wager that just about everyone here, when they first heard it, said it must be the craziest idea ever,” said John Kohut, chairman and CEO of Sea Dragon Energy. “I know I did when I first heard it.”

On Wednesday, Kohut spoke to a group of community and business leaders at a traditional Hawaiian blessing the company held at its warehouse located at the Hawai‘i Ocean Science Technology Park in Kailua-Kona that is operated by the Natural Energy Laboratory of Hawaiʻi Authority.
Suzanne Shaske, director of operations of engineering at Sea Dragon, led a tour of the facility’s emerging fuel-production technology.

“Today’s milestone represents an important step in Sea Dragon’s proof-of-capability program,” Kohut said. “Producing our first fuel demonstrates the advancement of our efforts to develop distributed, modular and scalable systems capable of producing fuel at or near the point of need.”

The large facility is not producing fuel yet, but the company expects it will have samples created by early 2027. The long-term goal is to create fuel on a barge at sea that would be used by the military.
Kohut said seawater-to-jet fuel is based on sound science and technologies, some of which were invented more than 100 years ago, and others that are much more recent.
Jet fuel is a combination of certain hydrocarbon molecules made up of hydrogen and carbon.
There are seven major steps that Sea Dragon will be integrating at the facility and proving so they can ultimately scale up.
“The bottom line is, first, you extract carbon dioxide from seawater and ultimately convert it into carbon monoxide,” Kohut said. “Also, from water, you can get hydrogen.”

With the carbon and hydrogen, engineers at Sea Dragon will use the Fischer-Tropsch skid to produce hydrocarbons. From there, Sea Dragon will refine, distill and get the right mix of hydrocarbons and additives to meet the requirements for specific jet fuels.

The technology breakthrough to convert seawater to jet fuel was developed by the U.S. Naval Research Laboratory in 2014. The Navy then awarded a $9.4 million contract to Sea Dragon Energy in August 2025 to fund the research into what it would take to develop the jet fuel on scale, according to the U.S. Department of War.

“Not to be melodramatic, but today you’re witnessing that next step of a very collective and engaged and resilient partnership as we challenge our Sea Dragon teammates to move the dream of science into reality of jet fuel,” said Mat Winter, retired vice admiral from the U.S. Navy.

Winter told the group he had a front-row seat to the discovery in 2014. He was working hand-in-hand with the Naval Research Laboratory scientists who were taking the seawater-to-jet-fuel science and putting it together so companies, specifically Sea Dragon, could then license, mature and produce it.

“As we look at this science and, I’ll say, transition to reality, you’re going to realize that this is a pivotal change for our Navy,” Winter said. “The ability to actually provide the fuels needed at the point of need (on the sea). That’s an incredible opportunity.”
While it’s still in the exploratory phase to determine if jet fuel created from water will be able to be produced on a large scale, Winter said, Sea Dragon will take that dream and move it forward.
“It’s much more mature than it has been,” Winter said.

With the technologies developed, Sea Dragon has chosen to set up shop at Kona’s technology park to prove the concept of seawater to jet fuel works. The company’s mission is to address a critical challenge for military operations and remote communities: the dependence on extensive, often vulnerable fuel-supply chains.
By developing technology that produces drop-in aviation fuel from seawater and power, the company seeks to reduce logistics burdens, strengthen fuel independence and enhance operational readiness.

“Over the last four years or more, we’ve been on contract under the Office of Naval Research to develop these technologies, to integrate this together, and demonstrate the capability, and prove that this type of fuel can, in fact, be totally synthesized from seawater,” Kohut said.
In the next two years, the energy company hopes to refine the technology, work with catalysts and try to figure out how they can produce the fuel as efficiently as possible.
“Because that’s the name of the game,” Kohut said. “It’s efficiency. It’s ultimately, how much does a gallon of jet fuel cost when we’re complete with the process?”
Also, Kohut said the other big piece is how that fuel is being delivered.
“The next step is to move from here onto a barge,” he told the group. “Our plan is to move this technology onto maritime vessels.”
Keith Olson, interim executive director of the Natural Energy Laboratory of Hawaiʻi Authority, said the state agency provides deep and surface-sea water to clients at the technology park.

What the authority tries to do, Olson said, is bring in new companies, like Sea Dragon, that would utilize either the deep or the surface-sea water or both, and then create new technologies and a business, which would then be employing people that live here on the island.
“They fit perfectly because they’re going to be utilizing our deep-ocean water for their feed for the CO2 (carbon dioxide) that they need to create,” Olson said.
Hawai‘i U.S. Rep. Jill Tokuda was among the guest speakers on Wednesday. She noted that as she flew into the Big Island, she has officially flown a million miles.
“I literally run on jet fuel, and a lot of Kona coffee,” Tokuda said with a laugh.

But on a more serious note, she said: “It reminds me how important it is to have safe, responsible jet fuel being produced throughout our country, throughout our world, and especially right here on our islands.”

Tokuda said the Big Island and the state have had a rough year, with communities suffering damage from Kona low storms to an earthquake in South Kona to Hurricanes Lala, Lowell and Nolo. These disasters are a reminder of the critical need to ensure the islands have access to resources.

“When I think about companies like Sea Dragon Energy, when I think about the groundbreaking work and research that you will do here, I can’t help but think about the greatest resource we will bring to the table and to your endeavors: our people,” Tokuda said. “The very best and the brightest you will find anywhere in the world, I would argue, totally biased, but the ones that we want to make sure can see a future for themselves right here at home in Hawaiʻi.”
Tokuda said too many keiki (children) think they have to travel a million miles away to find opportunities.

extraction.body: A Texas company has plans to use a site at the Natural Energy Laboratory of Hawaii Authority’s Hawaii Ocean Science and Technology Park in Kailua-Kona to make jet fuel from seawater. A Texas company has plans to use a site at the Natural Energy Laboratory of Hawaii Authority’s Hawaii Ocean Science and Technology Park in Kailua-Kona to make jet fuel from seawater. The state’s Office of Planning and Sustainable Development on Monday published a draft environmental assessment with a finding of no significant environmental impact for the project proposal by Sea Dragon Energy Inc. of Florence, Texas, a small town about 40 miles north of Austin. “Our desire is to meet the specifications for JP-5,” Tracy Kriewald, Sea Dragon Energy’s vice president of engineering, told the Tribune-Herald on Monday. Jet Propellant-5, also known as JP-5, is a type of jet fuel used in military aircraft, mostly Navy aircraft that take off and land from aircraft carriers. It’s a flammable liquid that smells like kerosene and is made from hydrocarbons, which are compounds found in crude oil. The facility, when and if built, would be a research-and-development laboratory for Sea Dragon’s Project GENESIS. According to Sea Dragon’s website, the aim of the project is to refine the efficiency of a technology patented by the Naval Research Laboratory to allow extraction of carbon dioxide from seawater and simultaneously produce hydrogen. “The ocean is an incredible reservoir with over 140 times the carbon dioxide concentration compared to air, and it also contains hydrogen, which is another important component in making SAF” — which is an acronym for “sustainable aviation fuel” — according to Sea Dragon’s website. Sea Dragon said the next-generation aviation fuel-making process will have both military and commercial applications. NELHA’s HOST Park extracts seawater from depths of up to 3,000 feet below the ocean’s surface which, according to Kriewald, is what makes the Kona site attractive to Sea Dragon. “We want to go there because they have great seawater and seawater infrastructure,” he said. “We want the nice, clean seawater to make it easier for us. “We won’t have to do a lot of pre-treatment of the water.” While the potential of the project appears to be as vast as the ocean itself, the technology is in its infancy. According to the draft EA, the process will require the monthly extraction of 449,000 gallons of seawater through NELHA’s seawater system, 50,000 gallons of fresh water, and 70 kilograms of supplemental hydrogen (H2) gas to produce 10 gallons of aviation fuel. Byproducts of the process will include hydrocarbon gases equivalent to a gallon of fuel and 80 gallons of water. According to Kriewald, the seawater and fresh water will be returned to the source — the ocean, in the case of the seawater. The fresh water might come from the Department of Water Supply, although the document indicates an alternative source is being considered. The supplemental hydrogen could come from a production facility at the HOST Park, although commercial alternatives also are available. “For every gallon of ocean water that we use, we put a gallon back in. We don’t use any water. We just extract the CO2 that’s embedded in it,” Kriewald said. The facility, which is projected to cost between $12 million and $20 million, would be built in an already existing building that formerly housed a bottler of desalinated seawater. “No new buildings, substantial land disturbances, or substantial new outdoor equipment are proposed,” the draft EA states. Project GENESIS, if successful, could lead to the development of a larger seawater-to-jet fuel industry. “This might be the first integrated end-to-end process that we know of, in which one company is responsible for everything for direct ocean capture,” Kriewald said. “But this is not a manufacturing facility, at all. That’s not our job. “This project is to learn how to improve efficiency.” According to the draft EA, Sea Dragon will be responsible for decommissioning the equipment at the facility at the completion of the R&D period. “We’re a research lab, and we’ll always be a research lab,” Kriewald said. “We’ll be there maybe four to five years to do research on different things as the technology changes. “It’s a very interesting technology, and it could be something that’s very valuable for the future.” Sea Dragon representatives, according to Kriewald, will be at the HOST Park’s 50th Anniversary Open House from 10 a.m. to 3 p.m. Saturday, Oct. 19. The draft EA, which can be found at bit.ly/4ehrY4q, triggers at 30-day public comment period.

extraction.body: Ilhan Omar's home this week, Homeland Security Investigations, isn't exactly a household name. But some Republicans hailed HSI last spring, as they sought to end a shutdown of its parent agency, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, following the fatal shootings of two U.S. citizens by federal immigration agents in Minnesota. When Democrats held up funding for ICE in a push for new guardrails on immigration raids, Senate Appropriations Chair Susan Collins, R-Maine, pointed to the work of HSI as a key reason for ending the shutdown. "More than a quarter of ICE's annual appropriated budget is for Homeland Security Investigations, referred to as HSI," Collins said in a March 12 floor speech. "HSI's agents are tasked with combating cartels, human smuggling, child exploitation, forced labor and investigating international financial crimes," she said. "Do we really want to defund those vital investigations, Mr. I think not." But Democrats held firm, as some noted that HSI, along with Customs and Border Protection, plays a role in immigration enforcement. Murphy of Connecticut, the ranking Democrat on the Homeland Security Appropriations Subcommittee, told reporters in March, referring to the immigration crackdown. "So, you can't pretend that you're not funding immigration enforcement if you're funding CBP and HSI with no strings attached.” It remains unclear whether the investigation of Omar, a Minnesota Democrat, falls within the spectrum of work typically conducted by HSI. Since the probe burst into public view with Monday's raid, just weeks before the midterm elections, officials have offered no details on the investigation. “Homeland Security Investigations executed a judicially authorized search warrant secured by the Department of Justice,” the Justice Department said in a statement. “This enforcement action is part of an ongoing federal criminal investigation.” According to published reports, the probe centers on immigration paperwork that Omar used to secure legal status and ultimately U.S. citizenship. Omar has said she fled Somalia as a child with her family as the country was gripped by civil war. The Washington Post reported this week that officials are examining whether Omar or her father intentionally misstated her birth date on immigration paperwork so she could be eligible to derive citizenship through him as a minor when he was naturalized. Collins declined to comment on HSI's investigation of Omar. The Maine Republican weathered a storm of protests over immigration enforcement in July after a fatal shooting by an ICE agent in her home state. Democratic appropriators also did not respond, although House Democratic leaders issued a statement Monday saying the probe "raises serious questions about the continued corrupt weaponization of the federal government against Donald Trump’s adversaries." Omar dismissed the probe as politically motivated. "For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns," she wrote on X. "This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation." Wide-ranging mission As the investigative arm of the Department of Homeland Security, HSI has a wide portfolio ranging from probing violations of customs and immigration law to transnational crime, national security threats, terrorism, drug smuggling, child exploitation, human trafficking, illegal arms dealing and financial crimes. HSI’s workforce of over 10,400 employees includes more than 7,100 special agents assigned across the United States and in 53 countries, according to its website. The last time that appropriators from both parties outlined specific priorities for the agency was in 2024, under the Biden administration. They stressed the importance of combating transnational crime overseas, countering fentanyl, fighting child exploitation, and investigating forced labor, including of children, in a joint explanatory statement that accompanied a fiscal 2024 Homeland Security appropriations law. That law provided $2.46 billion for the investigations agency. A partisan impasse over immigration enforcement techniques triggered a 76-day shutdown of the Homeland Security Department in mid-February, when the House and Senate couldn't agree on a fiscal 2026 Homeland Security appropriations bill. Most of the department finally reopened at the end of April, when Congress agreed to pass funding for everything except immigration enforcement agencies, which included ICE and its HSI division. To fund those agencies, along with Customs and Border Protection, without any new curbs on immigration agents, Republicans drafted a partisan reconciliation bill that could be passed without the risk of a Democratic filibuster. That bill included $7.45 billion for HSI, a sum designed to fully fund the investigative agency for the next three years. When lawmakers return to Washington for a lame-duck session next month, the fight over immigration enforcement is sure to resume — particularly if Democrats gain clout in the midterm elections. "The American people deserve transparency, and we will deliver full accountability for the rogue abuse of power from the Department of Homeland Security and Department of Justice," House Democratic leaders said in a joint statement.

extraction.body: Ilhan Omar's home this week, Homeland Security Investigations, isn't exactly a household name. But some Republicans hailed HSI last spring, as they sought to end a shutdown of its parent agency, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, following the fatal shootings of two U.S. citizens by federal immigration agents in Minnesota. When Democrats held up funding for ICE in a push for new guardrails on immigration raids, Senate Appropriations Chair Susan Collins, R-Maine, pointed to the work of HSI as a key reason for ending the shutdown. "More than a quarter of ICE's annual appropriated budget is for Homeland Security Investigations, referred to as HSI," Collins said in a March 12 floor speech. "HSI's agents are tasked with combating cartels, human smuggling, child exploitation, forced labor and investigating international financial crimes," she said. "Do we really want to defund those vital investigations, Mr. I think not." But Democrats held firm, as some noted that HSI, along with Customs and Border Protection, plays a role in immigration enforcement. Murphy of Connecticut, the ranking Democrat on the Homeland Security Appropriations Subcommittee, told reporters in March, referring to the immigration crackdown. "So, you can't pretend that you're not funding immigration enforcement if you're funding CBP and HSI with no strings attached.” It remains unclear whether the investigation of Omar, a Minnesota Democrat, falls within the spectrum of work typically conducted by HSI. Since the probe burst into public view with Monday's raid, just weeks before the midterm elections, officials have offered no details on the investigation. “Homeland Security Investigations executed a judicially authorized search warrant secured by the Department of Justice,” the Justice Department said in a statement. “This enforcement action is part of an ongoing federal criminal investigation.” According to published reports, the probe centers on immigration paperwork that Omar used to secure legal status and ultimately U.S. citizenship. Omar has said she fled Somalia as a child with her family as the country was gripped by civil war. The Washington Post reported this week that officials are examining whether Omar or her father intentionally misstated her birth date on immigration paperwork so she could be eligible to derive citizenship through him as a minor when he was naturalized. Collins declined to comment on HSI's investigation of Omar. The Maine Republican weathered a storm of protests over immigration enforcement in July after a fatal shooting by an ICE agent in her home state. Democratic appropriators also did not respond, although House Democratic leaders issued a statement Monday saying the probe "raises serious questions about the continued corrupt weaponization of the federal government against Donald Trump’s adversaries." Omar dismissed the probe as politically motivated. "For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns," she wrote on X. "This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation." Wide-ranging mission As the investigative arm of the Department of Homeland Security, HSI has a wide portfolio ranging from probing violations of customs and immigration law to transnational crime, national security threats, terrorism, drug smuggling, child exploitation, human trafficking, illegal arms dealing and financial crimes. HSI’s workforce of over 10,400 employees includes more than 7,100 special agents assigned across the United States and in 53 countries, according to its website. The last time that appropriators from both parties outlined specific priorities for the agency was in 2024, under the Biden administration. They stressed the importance of combating transnational crime overseas, countering fentanyl, fighting child exploitation, and investigating forced labor, including of children, in a joint explanatory statement that accompanied a fiscal 2024 Homeland Security appropriations law. That law provided $2.46 billion for the investigations agency. A partisan impasse over immigration enforcement techniques triggered a 76-day shutdown of the Homeland Security Department in mid-February, when the House and Senate couldn't agree on a fiscal 2026 Homeland Security appropriations bill. Most of the department finally reopened at the end of April, when Congress agreed to pass funding for everything except immigration enforcement agencies, which included ICE and its HSI division. To fund those agencies, along with Customs and Border Protection, without any new curbs on immigration agents, Republicans drafted a partisan reconciliation bill that could be passed without the risk of a Democratic filibuster. That bill included $7.45 billion for HSI, a sum designed to fully fund the investigative agency for the next three years. When lawmakers return to Washington for a lame-duck session next month, the fight over immigration enforcement is sure to resume — particularly if Democrats gain clout in the midterm elections. "The American people deserve transparency, and we will deliver full accountability for the rogue abuse of power from the Department of Homeland Security and Department of Justice," House Democratic leaders said in a joint statement.

extraction.body: Red Uptober? Crypto Liquidations Top $1 Billion as Bitcoin, Ethereum and Solana Erase Gains October got off to a hot start, but the historically strong month for Bitcoin and crypto prices—called "Uptober" by many investors—hit a roadblock Friday thanks to President Trump's trade war. And now prices are falling fast as liquidations pile up. More than $1 billion worth of crypto positions have been liquidated over the last 24 hours, per data from CoinGlass, as crypto prices plunge alongside stocks following Trump's Friday morning declaration that "massive" tariffs against China are in the works. Bitcoin plunged from a price above $122,000 Friday morning to about $116,200 recently, down 4% on the day, while Ethereum has fallen almost 8% to about $3,975 and Solana has dipped over 7% on the day to $205. With those declines, Bitcoin has nearly erased all of its October gains, returning to a price last seen on October 1, while Ethereum and Solana both hit October lows on Friday per data from CoinGecko. October has historically been a particularly strong month for Bitcoin’s price—a longstanding pattern that has led much of the crypto industry to expect the same results come every fall. The trend at first seemed poised to continue this year; the first week of this month, BTC surged some 10.5% to a new all-time high price north of $126,000 . But this week, those gains started to fall off. And on Friday, they were nearly entirely erased after President Trump announced he was calling off a planned meeting with Chinese president Xi Jinping, ordering a “massive increase” of tariffs on Chinese goods entering the United States, in a move even he conceded could be “potentially painful” for Americans. Trump’s sharp words also spooked the stock market. The Nasdaq is deep in the red Friday, down about 3.5%, while the S&P 500 has fallen about 2.7%. The Dow is down 1.9%. But perhaps the most impacted asset of the day is Trump’s own crypto token. WLFI, the native token of World Liberty Financial, the Trump family’s crypto platform, plummeted over 17% immediately following the president’s China announcement, to just north of $0.14 a token. It has since partially recovered to $0.16. Editor's note: This story was updated after publication with additional details. © 2026 Decrypt Media, Inc. All rights reserved
passages: Red Uptober? Crypto Liquidations Top $1 Billion as Bitcoin, Ethereum and Solana Erase Gains

October got off to a hot start, but the historically strong month for Bitcoin and crypto prices—called "Uptober" by many investors—hit a roadblock Friday thanks to President Trump's trade war. And now prices are falling fast as liquidations pile up.

More than $1 billion worth of crypto positions have been liquidated over the last 24 hours, per data from CoinGlass, as crypto prices plunge alongside stocks following Trump's Friday morning declaration that "massive" tariffs against China are in the works.

Bitcoin plunged from a price above $122,000 Friday morning to about $116,200 recently, down 4% on the day, while Ethereum has fallen almost 8% to about $3,975 and Solana has dipped over 7% on the day to $205.

With those declines, Bitcoin has nearly erased all of its October gains, returning to a price last seen on October 1, while Ethereum and Solana both hit October lows on Friday per data from CoinGecko.

October has historically been a particularly strong month for Bitcoin’s price—a longstanding pattern that has led much of the crypto industry to expect the same results come every fall. The trend at first seemed poised to continue this year; the first week of this month, BTC surged some 10.5% to a new all-time high price north of $126,000 .

But this week, those gains started to fall off. And on Friday, they were nearly entirely erased after President Trump announced he was calling off a planned meeting with Chinese president Xi Jinping, ordering a “massive increase” of tariffs on Chinese goods entering the United States, in a move even he conceded could be “potentially painful” for Americans.
Trump’s sharp words also spooked the stock market. The Nasdaq is deep in the red Friday, down about 3.5%, while the S&P 500 has fallen about 2.7%. The Dow is down 1.9%.

But perhaps the most impacted asset of the day is Trump’s own crypto token. REGISTER NOW Security researchers at digital rights unit The Citizen Lab say government spyware makers are abusing global advertising networks to target and hack devices by serving malicious online adverts. A new report published Thursday by the University of Toronto lab, which investigates surveillance and digital rights abuses, said an Israeli company called Discover-Tech allows spyware makers to use its advertising platform to target specific people or devices almost anywhere in the world with spyware capable of invisibly stealing their data. The researchers say Discover-Tech presents itself as a legitimate advertising firm, but instead serves as a “bridge between ad vendors and the mercenary spyware ecosystem.” Citizen Lab said at least two makers of zero-click spyware, Candiru and Bindecy, used Discover-Tech’s platform to target people. Both of these spyware makers provide surveillance products that can infect devices without the victim having to open a message or click on a link. The researchers found that one attack affected at least 45 Windows computers at media organization Al Jazeera. The devices were apparently hacked in 2024 and 2025 via Candiru’s spyware after being exposed to online ads packed with malicious code. Citizen Lab said it wasn’t clear which governments were behind the attacks, but said this is the first confirmation of zero-click government-backed spyware attacks being delivered through online ads, potentially putting a vast number of devices around the world at risk of being targeted and hacked. “There has been a lot of buzz that online ads can be used to identify and automatically hack targets with pinpoint precision, but now for the first time, we have concrete technical evidence showing this process in action,” said Bill Marczak, a Citizen Lab senior researcher, ahead of the report’s release. Hackers have long sought ways to abuse access to advertising networks, in part because of their ability to reach almost any internet-connected device in the world. Ad networks are designed to help advertisers target certain kinds of people, devices, and organizations with specific ads, but they can also be abused to target specific individuals or devices with malicious code. While such so-called “malvertising” attacks are not new, using online ads to allow powerful government spyware to silently hack into devices is a notable escalation. Security and privacy experts have for years encouraged people to install ad-blockers to prevent ads from being displayed on desktop and mobile screens, including within apps . But the ubiquity of online advertising makes it difficult to escape the industry’s clutches entirely. The researchers said Discover-Tech’s platform, which the company calls Controlium, left some of its source code exposed on its login pages, allowing the researchers to recreate its web-based control panel dashboard without needing to log in. The researchers say the web dashboard “appears to be specifically designed to allow them to push malicious content to individual targeted users alongside advertisements.” Citizen Lab also found that Discover-Tech’s site had a publicly accessible portion that allowed the researchers to download reams of user login records for the Controlium dashboard without needing a password. Some login details belonged to at least two employees of spyware maker Candiru, as well as some from Bindecy. The researchers also found billions of ad bidding records left exposed on Discover-Tech’s website, which showed that its ads had ultimately been displayed across tens of thousands of mobile apps and websites between March and June 2026. The bidding records show that the ads were shown on devices used by militaries, governments, critical infrastructure, and national cyber agencies. However, it’s unclear if the displayed ads resulted in a compromise or infection. Security researchers with ad quality platform Confiant, which worked with Citizen Lab to investigate, said they found evidence that potentially malicious ads were similarly shown on devices on the networks of the International Atomic Energy Agency and the International Criminal Court. Citizen Lab’s Marczak said Discover-Tech is “surely just the tip of the iceberg,” and urged people to take defensive action. “If you might be targeted based on who you are or what you do, it’s time to disable ad tracking on your devices or even block ads altogether,” said Marczak. Al Jazeera did not respond to a request for comment about the hacks. Neither did Discover-Tech, and Candiru maker Integrity Labs could not be reached for comment. Security researchers at digital rights unit The Citizen Lab say government spyware makers are abusing global advertising networks to target and hack devices by serving malicious online adverts.

A new report published Thursday by the University of Toronto lab, which investigates surveillance and digital rights abuses, said an Israeli company called Discover-Tech allows spyware makers to use its advertising platform to target specific people or devices almost anywhere in the world with spyware capable of invisibly stealing their data.
The researchers say Discover-Tech presents itself as a legitimate advertising firm, but instead serves as a “bridge between ad vendors and the mercenary spyware ecosystem.”

Citizen Lab said at least two makers of zero-click spyware, Candiru and Bindecy, used Discover-Tech’s platform to target people. Both of these spyware makers provide surveillance products that can infect devices without the victim having to open a message or click on a link.

The researchers found that one attack affected at least 45 Windows computers at media organization Al Jazeera. The devices were apparently hacked in 2024 and 2025 via Candiru’s spyware after being exposed to online ads packed with malicious code.

Citizen Lab said it wasn’t clear which governments were behind the attacks, but said this is the first confirmation of zero-click government-backed spyware attacks being delivered through online ads, potentially putting a vast number of devices around the world at risk of being targeted and hacked.

“There has been a lot of buzz that online ads can be used to identify and automatically hack targets with pinpoint precision, but now for the first time, we have concrete technical evidence showing this process in action,” said Bill Marczak, a Citizen Lab senior researcher, ahead of the report’s release.

Hackers have long sought ways to abuse access to advertising networks, in part because of their ability to reach almost any internet-connected device in the world. Ad networks are designed to help advertisers target certain kinds of people, devices, and organizations with specific ads, but they can also be abused to target specific individuals or devices with malicious code.
While such so-called “malvertising” attacks are not new, using online ads to allow powerful government spyware to silently hack into devices is a notable escalation.

Security and privacy experts have for years encouraged people to install ad-blockers to prevent ads from being displayed on desktop and mobile screens, including within apps . But the ubiquity of online advertising makes it difficult to escape the industry’s clutches entirely.

The researchers said Discover-Tech’s platform, which the company calls Controlium, left some of its source code exposed on its login pages, allowing the researchers to recreate its web-based control panel dashboard without needing to log in. The researchers say the web dashboard “appears to be specifically designed to allow them to push malicious content to individual targeted users alongside advertisements.”

Citizen Lab also found that Discover-Tech’s site had a publicly accessible portion that allowed the researchers to download reams of user login records for the Controlium dashboard without needing a password. Some login details belonged to at least two employees of spyware maker Candiru, as well as some from Bindecy.

The researchers also found billions of ad bidding records left exposed on Discover-Tech’s website, which showed that its ads had ultimately been displayed across tens of thousands of mobile apps and websites between March and June 2026.

The bidding records show that the ads were shown on devices used by militaries, governments, critical infrastructure, and national cyber agencies. However, it’s unclear if the displayed ads resulted in a compromise or infection.

Security researchers with ad quality platform Confiant, which worked with Citizen Lab to investigate, said they found evidence that potentially malicious ads were similarly shown on devices on the networks of the International Atomic Energy Agency and the International Criminal Court.
Citizen Lab’s Marczak said Discover-Tech is “surely just the tip of the iceberg,” and urged people to take defensive action.
“If you might be targeted based on who you are or what you do, it’s time to disable ad tracking on your devices or even block ads altogether,” said Marczak.
Al Jazeera did not respond to a request for comment about the hacks. Neither did Discover-Tech, and Candiru maker Integrity Labs could not be reached for comment.

REGISTER NOW Security researchers at digital rights unit The Citizen Lab say government spyware makers are abusing global advertising networks to target and hack devices by serving malicious online adverts. A new report published Thursday by the University of Toronto lab, which investigates surveillance and digital rights abuses, said an Israeli company called Discover-Tech allows spyware makers to use its advertising platform to target specific people or devices almost anywhere in the world with spyware capable of invisibly stealing their data. The researchers say Discover-Tech presents itself as a legitimate advertising firm, but instead serves as a “bridge between ad vendors and the mercenary spyware ecosystem.” Citizen Lab said at least two makers of zero-click spyware, Candiru and Bindecy, used Discover-Tech’s platform to target people. Both of these spyware makers provide surveillance products that can infect devices without the victim having to open a message or click on a link. The researchers found that one attack affected at least 45 Windows computers at media organization Al Jazeera. The devices were apparently hacked in 2024 and 2025 via Candiru’s spyware after being exposed to online ads packed with malicious code. Citizen Lab said it wasn’t clear which governments were behind the attacks, but said this is the first confirmation of zero-click government-backed spyware attacks being delivered through online ads, potentially putting a vast number of devices around the world at risk of being targeted and hacked. “There has been a lot of buzz that online ads can be used to identify and automatically hack targets with pinpoint precision, but now for the first time, we have concrete technical evidence showing this process in action,” said Bill Marczak, a Citizen Lab senior researcher, ahead of the report’s release. Hackers have long sought ways to abuse access to advertising networks, in part because of their ability to reach almost any internet-connected device in the world. Ad networks are designed to help advertisers target certain kinds of people, devices, and organizations with specific ads, but they can also be abused to target specific individuals or devices with malicious code. While such so-called “malvertising” attacks are not new, using online ads to allow powerful government spyware to silently hack into devices is a notable escalation. Security and privacy experts have for years encouraged people to install ad-blockers to prevent ads from being displayed on desktop and mobile screens, including within apps . But the ubiquity of online advertising makes it difficult to escape the industry’s clutches entirely. The researchers said Discover-Tech’s platform, which the company calls Controlium, left some of its source code exposed on its login pages, allowing the researchers to recreate its web-based control panel dashboard without needing to log in. The researchers say the web dashboard “appears to be specifically designed to allow them to push malicious content to individual targeted users alongside advertisements.” Citizen Lab also found that Discover-Tech’s site had a publicly accessible portion that allowed the researchers to download reams of user login records for the Controlium dashboard without needing a password. Some login details belonged to at least two employees of spyware maker Candiru, as well as some from Bindecy. The researchers also found billions of ad bidding records left exposed on Discover-Tech’s website, which showed that its ads had ultimately been displayed across tens of thousands of mobile apps and websites between March and June 2026. The bidding records show that the ads were shown on devices used by militaries, governments, critical infrastructure, and national cyber agencies. However, it’s unclear if the displayed ads resulted in a compromise or infection. Security researchers with ad quality platform Confiant, which worked with Citizen Lab to investigate, said they found evidence that potentially malicious ads were similarly shown on devices on the networks of the International Atomic Energy Agency and the International Criminal Court. Citizen Lab’s Marczak said Discover-Tech is “surely just the tip of the iceberg,” and urged people to take defensive action. “If you might be targeted based on who you are or what you do, it’s time to disable ad tracking on your devices or even block ads altogether,” said Marczak. Al Jazeera did not respond to a request for comment about the hacks. Neither did Discover-Tech, and Candiru maker Integrity Labs could not be reached for comment. extraction.body: Incident hitting 700 supermarkets exploited outdated devices exposed to the Internet. Earlier this week, a mass hack of refrigeration systems at an estimated 700 supermarkets throughout France caused them to suddenly malfunction, causing spoilage of untold tons of perishables and, in some cases, fires. As is now the norm, basic cybersecurity would have prevented it. French authorities say the systems, made up of entire fleets of refrigerators and freezers throughout a store, were hacked. More specifically, Internet-connected controllers that allow technicians to remotely administer the store-wide systems were compromised. The unknown attackers responsible then activated defrosters long enough for the fridges to reach temperatures as high as 50° Celsius (122° Fahrenheit). By the time the mass compromise was discovered, food was spoiled, and in some cases their electrical systems caught fire. Multiple security advisories and public research reports show that all three of the controller models reportedly hacked in the incident—sold by Danfoss of Denmark and Dixell and its parent company Copeland in the US—contained critical vulnerabilities that allow attackers to remotely log in to the devices with the same system rights as administrators. Until recently, Danfoss controllers, for instance, used a credential that changes each day. The password is generated by the publicly available firmware based on the date. A hacker who takes the time to analyze the code can do the same thing on any device that hasn’t received a recent update. Daily passwords are identical across models located in hundreds or thousands of stores. A raft of critical vulnerabilities fixed in the past few months in Copeland/Dixel controllers also give similar remote access. Besides running controllers with outdated firmware, the affected stores likely also failed to put the devices behind a VPN and create a restricted list of IP addresses allowed to log in. These protections are standard but often not followed. In this case, that failure enabled a mass hack that likely cost tens or hundreds of millions of euros. Spain, Portugal, Poland, Germany, and Belgium were also reportedly affected. “Two things would have changed the outcome,” researchers at Pen Test Partners said Wednesday. “Cyber hygiene would have prevented the access: take the controller off the public internet, put remote access behind a VPN and an IP allowlist, bring third-party kit onto the network in a controlled, owned and documented way rather than leaving it on a contractor’s own connection, change known and default credentials, and patch to a current release.” Researchers from security firm Claroty warned of the threat of ignoring these common-sense steps last October . The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency did the same in February. In an email, Copeland acknowledged a vulnerability “identified in a discontinued, end-of-life generation of controllers” and said the company is working with customers to prevent similar incidents in the future. Danfoss representatives didn’t immediately respond to questions. CNN said the company also cited discontinued models. So far, the party behind the attack has remained silent. That raises the possibility that the motive was vandalism on a mass scale. Another possibility is a nation-state or other international actor aiming to create a continent-wide disruption. The incident underscores the tension between the financial and security departments in most businesses. Some companies are loath to spend large sums of money on new equipment when there are no tangible benefits or savings. Only after a devastating hack do they realize why the investment was worthwhile. Executives at affected supermarket chains will likely learn the hard lessons. Less clear is whether the cautionary tale will sway other businesses. extraction.body: Incident hitting 700 supermarkets exploited outdated devices exposed to the Internet. Earlier this week, a mass hack of refrigeration systems at an estimated 700 supermarkets throughout France caused them to suddenly malfunction, causing spoilage of untold tons of perishables and, in some cases, fires. As is now the norm, basic cybersecurity would have prevented it. French authorities say the systems, made up of entire fleets of refrigerators and freezers throughout a store, were hacked. More specifically, Internet-connected controllers that allow technicians to remotely administer the store-wide systems were compromised. The unknown attackers responsible then activated defrosters long enough for the fridges to reach temperatures as high as 50° Celsius (122° Fahrenheit). By the time the mass compromise was discovered, food was spoiled, and in some cases their electrical systems caught fire. Multiple security advisories and public research reports show that all three of the controller models reportedly hacked in the incident—sold by Danfoss of Denmark and Dixell and its parent company Copeland in the US—contained critical vulnerabilities that allow attackers to remotely log in to the devices with the same system rights as administrators. Until recently, Danfoss controllers, for instance, used a credential that changes each day. The password is generated by the publicly available firmware based on the date. A hacker who takes the time to analyze the code can do the same thing on any device that hasn’t received a recent update. Daily passwords are identical across models located in hundreds or thousands of stores. A raft of critical vulnerabilities fixed in the past few months in Copeland/Dixel controllers also give similar remote access. Besides running controllers with outdated firmware, the affected stores likely also failed to put the devices behind a VPN and create a restricted list of IP addresses allowed to log in. These protections are standard but often not followed. In this case, that failure enabled a mass hack that likely cost tens or hundreds of millions of euros. Spain, Portugal, Poland, Germany, and Belgium were also reportedly affected. “Two things would have changed the outcome,” researchers at Pen Test Partners said Wednesday. “Cyber hygiene would have prevented the access: take the controller off the public internet, put remote access behind a VPN and an IP allowlist, bring third-party kit onto the network in a controlled, owned and documented way rather than leaving it on a contractor’s own connection, change known and default credentials, and patch to a current release.” Researchers from security firm Claroty warned of the threat of ignoring these common-sense steps last October . The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency did the same in February. In an email, Copeland acknowledged a vulnerability “identified in a discontinued, end-of-life generation of controllers” and said the company is working with customers to prevent similar incidents in the future. Danfoss representatives didn’t immediately respond to questions. CNN said the company also cited discontinued models. So far, the party behind the attack has remained silent. That raises the possibility that the motive was vandalism on a mass scale. Another possibility is a nation-state or other international actor aiming to create a continent-wide disruption. The incident underscores the tension between the financial and security departments in most businesses. Some companies are loath to spend large sums of money on new equipment when there are no tangible benefits or savings. Only after a devastating hack do they realize why the investment was worthwhile. Executives at affected supermarket chains will likely learn the hard lessons. Less clear is whether the cautionary tale will sway other businesses. extraction.body: Last two days at Disrupt are half off. Don’t miss any more moments. REGISTER NOW Rivian recently rolled out an AI assistant that lets drivers and passengers interact with the company’s electric vehicles just by talking to them. But the carmaker’s founder and CEO, RJ Scaringe, said at TechCrunch Disrupt this week that, in the future, Rivian’s cars will be able to run AI agents made by other companies like Anthropic. “That’s where it becomes magical,” Scaringe said onstage. Scaringe didn’t say when Rivian would implement this, and the company declined to offer more details, pointing instead to the “AI & Autonomy Day” event it’s hosting in December. But it’s not hard to imagine how Rivian might integrate something like Claude, OpenAI’s Dots, or Meta’s Muse assistant into its software. The company has developed its in-car software from the ground up, instead of leaning on Apple CarPlay or Android Auto, and built a lot of its own applications, like navigation (though it has worked to integrate popular in-car apps like Apple Music). Rivian says it has created its own in-house agentic framework that understands what action a person wants to take when they talk to the vehicle, and routes it to the right part of the car’s software. Most of the time, that involves what you’d expect: asking the car to turn down the temperature, activate the seat warmers, or summarize the news. “Think of it as like a traffic light. So if you ask the vehicle something, it decides what model it’s going to use. It can use a local model that’s running on the edge and the vehicle. If it’s a more complex question, it can go up to the cloud. And then even for that, we have different models that we use,” Scaringe said. As of May of this year, the agent could access external apps like Google Calendar. And Scaringe said at Disrupt the next step would be to add products from the frontier AI companies, though making them work in the car won’t be easy. “There’s a lot of plumbing behind the scenes we have to do to make sure that that works, and it’s not just within Rivian. That’s also a lot of coordination with the labs to make sure they enable that plumbing,” he said, adding that putting this kind of software near safety-critical systems means Rivian has to be extremely careful. “You wouldn’t want an agent to determine, ‘hey, it’s time to apply the brakes, or time to steer the vehicle.’ So anything that’s vehicle-level controls are not being handed to an agent,” he said. Instead, he thinks the implementation will look more like an extension of how people currently use these agentic apps. That would mean Rivian would have to find a way to connect the vehicle to all of the context that apps like Muse collect on their users. For example, Scaringe said, a driver could ask the Rivian assistant to turn on the ventilated seats before going deeper. “And then simultaneously say, ‘We were talking yesterday about this meal. I’m planning to have guests over on Friday. Can you help me think through what we’re going to make?’,” he said. The car could then pull the driver’s context from a conversation they had with the assistant on another device. Of course, Rivian wouldn’t be the first American car company to add AI agents to a car’s software. Earlier this year, Tesla added a feature that let users talk to both SpaceX’s Grok chatbot and also its Grok Bot assistant. sources.title: Flock CEO defends surveillance technology amid national backlash: ‘We shouldn’t pause progress’
passages: “If we want to live in a society where, if you commit a crime, you have a higher probability of being held accountable, we shouldn’t pause progress,” Langley said, speaking onstage during a panel at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 in San Francisco on Wednesday.
Flock’s founder and CEO Garrett Langley doesn’t think the risks of introducing surveillance technology at scale outweigh the rewards.
“Technology, at its core, in its definition, is just doing things better.
It’s not doing things perfect,” he said. “Driverless cars, I think, is a fair analogy.
The answer is to say, ‘Hey, let’s talk about how we prevent more accidents in the future’.”
But driverless car makers don’t shrug their shoulders at crashes; the companies pause their fleets and apply fixes.

During the interview, the controversial founder of the surveillance maker of license plate cameras and other recording devices deflected hard questions about the criticism Flock now faces — which has since led to canceled contracts and even layoffs .

Instead, Langley tended to respond to questions with anecdotes from conversations with police chiefs and city leaders across the United States, and tales of the supposed numerous crimes Flock has solved, rather than offer tangible solutions to people’s concerns.
Much like AI, Flock is a technology that some feel has been forced upon the public without their consent.
But pressed about abuse and the invasiveness of his company’s surveillance technology, Langley had no substantive answers.
“He was describing that, too often as a society we judge technology not on how it compares to the past, but how it compares to perfect.
For instance, he referenced a time when a customer ended their contract because they believed the devices performed facial recognition.
While Flock cameras do not have facial recognition, they do have the ability to detect and track people .

REGISTER NOW Flock’s founder and CEO Garrett Langley doesn’t think the risks of introducing surveillance technology at scale outweigh the rewards. “If we want to live in a society where, if you commit a crime, you have a higher probability of being held accountable, we shouldn’t pause progress,” Langley said, speaking onstage during a panel at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 in San Francisco on Wednesday. During the interview, the controversial founder of the surveillance maker of license plate cameras and other recording devices deflected hard questions about the criticism Flock now faces — which has since led to canceled contracts and even layoffs . Instead, Langley tended to respond to questions with anecdotes from conversations with police chiefs and city leaders across the United States, and tales of the supposed numerous crimes Flock has solved, rather than offer tangible solutions to people’s concerns. In doing so, Langley positioned Flock as an advance in technology that was somewhat inevitable. He stressed that if people wanted to live in a better society — that is, one with reduced crime — they would have to offer up their privacy in return. A similar argument about the trade-offs and rewards could be made for AI, which is marketed to the public as vastly improving our lives, automating tedious tasks, and making things more convenient. The flip side is the cost of sharing everything about ourselves with the makers of the AI agents themselves — and the possibility of the destruction of humanity , according to some. It’s no surprise that the AI backlash shares some overlap with Flock. Much like AI, Flock is a technology that some feel has been forced upon the public without their consent. For Langley, this is just the nature of progress, he explained. “Technology, at its core, in its definition, is just doing things better. It’s not doing things perfect,” he said. “Driverless cars, I think, is a fair analogy. Driverless cars, I think, are definitively safer than human drivers. And when there’s one accident, I don’t think the answer is to shut down driverless cars. The answer is to say, ‘Hey, let’s talk about how we prevent more accidents in the future’.” But driverless car makers don’t shrug their shoulders at crashes; the companies pause their fleets and apply fixes. Flock, meanwhile, seems to wrestle as a company with understanding when it’s the company’s responsibility to intervene. From Langley’s answers, it’s clear that the ethics around how Flock should be used is a decision he would much rather leave up to others. “We don’t want to tell city leaders how to do their job,” he noted. “We will provide recommendations, we’ll provide defaults, but we’re going to minimize the number of mandated features, functions, and policies,” he said. Among the many rebuttals to his critics that Langley raised during the interview was the idea that misinformation about Flock had led to some of its customers’ cancellations. For instance, he referenced a time when a customer ended their contract because they believed the devices performed facial recognition. While Flock cameras do not have facial recognition, they do have the ability to detect and track people . Langley also spent a fair amount of time admonishing those who think his technology, or any technology, should be perfect, attributing the quote to some unnamed community leader. “He was describing that, too often as a society we judge technology not on how it compares to the past, but how it compares to perfect. And Flock is far from perfect; I’m far from perfect — I’ve made plenty of mistakes,” Langley said. Another area of pushback was in positioning Flock as a more effective form of policing, and one that allowed police departments to do more with reduced staff. “If you look at where policing has gone over the last decade, but particularly post-COVID, law enforcement employment is declining rapidly. I think about a place like San Francisco, and there’s hundreds of open positions. They will probably never be filled,” he said, positioning Flock as the tech that would fill in those gaps. But pressed about abuse and the invasiveness of his company’s surveillance technology, Langley had no substantive answers. “I think if the idea is to curb abuse, I think there’s a way to do that that doesn’t disrupt the legal system, that doesn’t disrupt the efficacy and flow of a police department,” Langley said, without spelling out what those ideas were. For Langley, those seem to be matters of secondary importance, because his belief in Flock as a public good is so strong. “I think one of the unfortunate consequences of building a consequential company is this is the price you pay, and I think it’s worth it because there’s millions and millions of people who have a better life today because [of] Flock,” he said. “And clearly we’ve made our fair share of mistakes, and there’s some folks who disagree with what we do, but it’s worth it because one day they might be a victim,” Langley added. extraction.body: Last two days at Disrupt are half off. Don’t miss any more moments. REGISTER NOW Flock’s founder and CEO Garrett Langley doesn’t think the risks of introducing surveillance technology at scale outweigh the rewards. “If we want to live in a society where, if you commit a crime, you have a higher probability of being held accountable, we shouldn’t pause progress,” Langley said, speaking onstage during a panel at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 in San Francisco on Wednesday. During the interview, the controversial founder of the surveillance maker of license plate cameras and other recording devices deflected hard questions about the criticism Flock now faces — which has since led to canceled contracts and even layoffs . Instead, Langley tended to respond to questions with anecdotes from conversations with police chiefs and city leaders across the United States, and tales of the supposed numerous crimes Flock has solved, rather than offer tangible solutions to people’s concerns. In doing so, Langley positioned Flock as an advance in technology that was somewhat inevitable. He stressed that if people wanted to live in a better society — that is, one with reduced crime — they would have to offer up their privacy in return. A similar argument about the trade-offs and rewards could be made for AI, which is marketed to the public as vastly improving our lives, automating tedious tasks, and making things more convenient. The flip side is the cost of sharing everything about ourselves with the makers of the AI agents themselves — and the possibility of the destruction of humanity , according to some. It’s no surprise that the AI backlash shares some overlap with Flock. Much like AI, Flock is a technology that some feel has been forced upon the public without their consent. For Langley, this is just the nature of progress, he explained. “Technology, at its core, in its definition, is just doing things better. It’s not doing things perfect,” he said. “Driverless cars, I think, is a fair analogy. Driverless cars, I think, are definitively safer than human drivers. And when there’s one accident, I don’t think the answer is to shut down driverless cars. The answer is to say, ‘Hey, let’s talk about how we prevent more accidents in the future’.” But driverless car makers don’t shrug their shoulders at crashes; the companies pause their fleets and apply fixes. Flock, meanwhile, seems to wrestle as a company with understanding when it’s the company’s responsibility to intervene. From Langley’s answers, it’s clear that the ethics around how Flock should be used is a decision he would much rather leave up to others. “We don’t want to tell city leaders how to do their job,” he noted. “We will provide recommendations, we’ll provide defaults, but we’re going to minimize the number of mandated features, functions, and policies,” he said. Among the many rebuttals to his critics that Langley raised during the interview was the idea that misinformation about Flock had led to some of its customers’ cancellations. For instance, he referenced a time when a customer ended their contract because they believed the devices performed facial recognition. While Flock cameras do not have facial recognition, they do have the ability to detect and track people . Langley also spent a fair amount of time admonishing those who think his technology, or any technology, should be perfect, attributing the quote to some unnamed community leader. “He was describing that, too often as a society we judge technology not on how it compares to the past, but how it compares to perfect. And Flock is far from perfect; I’m far from perfect — I’ve made plenty of mistakes,” Langley said. Another area of pushback was in positioning Flock as a more effective form of policing, and one that allowed police departments to do more with reduced staff. “If you look at where policing has gone over the last decade, but particularly post-COVID, law enforcement employment is declining rapidly. I think about a place like San Francisco, and there’s hundreds of open positions. They will probably never be filled,” he said, positioning Flock as the tech that would fill in those gaps. But pressed about abuse and the invasiveness of his company’s surveillance technology, Langley had no substantive answers. “I think if the idea is to curb abuse, I think there’s a way to do that that doesn’t disrupt the legal system, that doesn’t disrupt the efficacy and flow of a police department,” Langley said, without spelling out what those ideas were. For Langley, those seem to be matters of secondary importance, because his belief in Flock as a public good is so strong. “I think one of the unfortunate consequences of building a consequential company is this is the price you pay, and I think it’s worth it because there’s millions and millions of people who have a better life today because [of] Flock,” he said. “And clearly we’ve made our fair share of mistakes, and there’s some folks who disagree with what we do, but it’s worth it because one day they might be a victim,” Langley added. sources.title: CedarDB wants one database to handle both transactions and analytics, as AI agents raise the stakes
passages: Databases have traditionally been built for one of two jobs.
Analytical databases help businesses spot trends and answer questions, while operational databases store the day-to-day records of transactions, like orders and payments.
But the Munich-based database engine CedarDB supports both, and its approach has gained relevance with the rise of agentic AI, its co-founder and CEO Moritz Sichert told TechCrunch.
CedarDB’s questioning of the divide between analytical and operational queries is a by-product of its focus on efficiency.

The company is a Technical University of Munich spinout based on Umbra , a research project that was built from scratch to beat legacy database engines at processing speed by making the most of modern hardware.
It is too early to tell how disruptive this might be, but Sichert interprets Databricks’ move as another sign that there is demand for what CedarDB does.
The startup plans to serve its first cloud users with its current team of 14 people, but Sichert expects it will need a larger team once it gets more traction.
“And this is where we would raise our next round.”

CedarDB has been in the making for the last decade, but its current momentum stems from enterprise companies whose existing data stacks may have been well suited to storing years of transactions, yet less suited to quickly answering analytical questions asked in natural language about that data.
According to Sichert, this compatibility with the popular database helps keep switching costs low, since users don’t need to rebuild their apps.
It also has an added advantage: CedarDB follows the logic LLMs are most familiar with as a result of their training.

With five Umbra researchers as its co-founders, CedarDB kept that approach, promising faster performance without requiring more CPUs or processing power and memory — and requiring few changes from customers.
In particular, its team made sure CedarDB was compatible with PostgreSQL , an open source database system.

In the end, it launched CedarDB Enterprise as an on-premise offering alongside its free version, CedarDB Community Edition, both announced in May of last year at the same time as it announced a €5.3 million seed funding round (approximately $6 million).
A fully managed, cloud-hosted version will likely help CedarDB expand its user base beyond large enterprises.
It will also make it better prepared to compete with the likes of Databricks, a major data company that seems to have reached the same conclusion as the German startup.

At its Data + AI Summit in June, the American company cited “the agentic era” as the reason why it was launching LTAP , a new data architecture aiming to “[unify] transactions, analytics, streaming, and operational data on a single copy of storage in the lake.”
Pictured from left to right: CedarDB founders Moritz Sichert, Lukas Vogel, Philipp Fent, Dominik Durner, and Christian Winter.

sources.title: Amazon’s Bee launches two new personal AI devices, starting at $75
passages: Amazon’s personal AI wearable maker, Bee , is announcing its first new products since being acquired by the retail giant last year .

The tech company on Thursday introduced the Bee Frontier, the next generation of its device that can be worn on the wrist or pinned to clothes, along with Bee Eclipse, a credit-card-sized device that magnetically attaches to the back of your smartphone.
In addition, you can opt to connect the Bee to Alexa, allowing your Echo device to use its ability to identify your voice, a feature called Voice ID, to recognize when you’re speaking.
To make all this possible, Bee devices use a private computing security architecture, which doesn’t store the raw audio from your conversations.
Instead, audio is processed in real time and then deleted.

Jio Platforms, the digital arm of Indian billionaire Mukesh Ambani’s Reliance Industries, is seeking to raise as much as $3.2 billion in what could be India’s biggest initial public offering. The listing will test public-market appetite for a company that attracted more than $20 billion from global investors, including Google and Meta in 2020.

On Wednesday, Reliance Industries said in a stock exchange filing (PDF) that Jio had set a price band of ₹1,065 to ₹1,119 (about $11.19 to $11.76) per share for the offering of up to 270 million new shares (PDF). The IPO will open for subscription on October 21 and close on October 23, with bidding for anchor investors scheduled for October 19.
At the upper end of the proposed price band, the IPO would value Jio at about ₹10.3 trillion (around $108.3 billion), based on the number of shares expected to be outstanding after the offering.
In 2020, Jio was valued at up to ₹4.91 trillion ( about $65 billion at the time). Meta, then known as Facebook, invested $5.7 billion , while Google committed $4.5 billion .

Jio’s IPO is set to overtake Hyundai Motor India’s ₹278.7 billion ($3.3 billion at the time) offering in 2024, the country’s biggest to date, even if its shares are priced at the lower end of the range.

Since launching in 2016, Jio has grown into India’s largest telecom operator, with more than 524 million subscribers as of March 31, ahead of Bharti Airtel, Vodafone Idea, and state-owned BSNL. It initially drew customers with free data and cheap plans, though its prices are now comparable to those of its rivals. Over time, Jio has grown beyond a telco and expanded into broadband , cloud services , and other digital businesses .

Jio’s IPO comes as Elon Musk has stepped up his criticism of Ambani , accusing him of trying to keep Starlink out of India. The accusation comes more than a year after Jio and rival Airtel signed deals with Musk’s SpaceX to distribute Starlink’s satellite internet service in India, subject to regulatory approvals. Indian authorities have rejected Musk’s claims .

In the quarter ended June, Jio’s revenue rose nearly 12% from a year earlier to ₹391.7 billion (about $4.1 billion), while its net profit climbed 9% to ₹77.6 billion (around $816 million), per its IPO prospectus (PDF).

Jio has set aside shares worth up to ₹25 billion (about $263 million) for eligible Reliance Industries shareholders and another ₹5 billion ($53 million) for employees, who will receive a discount of ₹54 per share.

Of the IPO proceeds, Jio plans to use up to ₹275 billion ($2.9 billion) to repay debt at its telecom subsidiary, Reliance Jio Infocomm, with the remaining proceeds going toward general corporate purposes, per the prospectus.

Jio Platforms, the digital arm of Indian billionaire Mukesh Ambani’s Reliance Industries, is seeking to raise as much as $3.2 billion in what could be India’s biggest initial public offering. The listing will test public-market appetite for a company that attracted more than $20 billion from global investors, including Google and Meta in 2020.

On Wednesday, Reliance Industries said in a stock exchange filing (PDF) that Jio had set a price band of ₹1,065 to ₹1,119 (about $11.19 to $11.76) per share for the offering of up to 270 million new shares (PDF). The IPO will open for subscription on October 21 and close on October 23, with bidding for anchor investors scheduled for October 19.
At the upper end of the proposed price band, the IPO would value Jio at about ₹10.3 trillion (around $108.3 billion), based on the number of shares expected to be outstanding after the offering.
In 2020, Jio was valued at up to ₹4.91 trillion ( about $65 billion at the time). Meta, then known as Facebook, invested $5.7 billion , while Google committed $4.5 billion .

But the team still needs to establish whether the approach could work for humans.
